By developing a distributed scheduling framework based on game theory, we effectively tackle this challenge and achieve an optimal solution that minimizes latency and meets demand. Furthermore, we design and evaluate a hybrid Proximity-Induced Reference Shape (PIRS) algorithm to illustrate the feasibility of our approach. Simulation results highlight the algorithm's performance and scalability in response to changing system conditions and increasing demand.

Despite extensive research on the Hall anomaly in type-II superconductors, particularly in BSCCO thin films, there remains an unexplained component of the Hall effect that cannot be accounted for by the normal metal layer at the surface or by vortex matter. Our study offers a detailed examination of the vortex phase diagram in BSCCO and precisely measures the vortex lattice relaxation length, lambda, as the distance between vortices in this lattice. We calculate the concentration of vacancies in the vortex lattice by measuring the angle-dependent Hall effect and compare this to the expected vacancy concentration based on the measured lambda and critical current. Our analysis suggests that increasing underdoping in BSCCO results in an increase in vacancy concentrations within the vortex lattice, offering quantitative data that can be utilized to refine physics models of vortex matter.

Researchers suggest using the parallel update algorithm for the Ising model to measure temperature fluctuations in three-dimensional systems. Previous work using this method for small systems revealed an unexpected fixed point at low temperatures, where all higher-order temperature fluctuations relative to a reference fluctuation (with a specific size) are zero. In the current study, we extend this research by examining larger systems up to the scaling size of $L=20$. Our findings show that in the low-temperature regime, all temperature fluctuations for a given size relative to the reference fluctuation decrease in proportion to $L^{-d}$, with $d=2.02\pm 0.01$. A similar analysis using the stochastic cluster algorithm produces analogous results. This study provides a direct method for determining critical temperatures and possibly even the specific heat capacity in small systems.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, specifically those that generate hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite depth, is provided, utilizing the index theory and a modified version of the square root invariant from classical subfactor theory.

Recent research involving Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) has been intriguing, as these novel models unexpectedly match the performance of established methods for tasks like time series prediction. Given their equivalence to Neural State Space models and their computationally efficient gradient calculations, it is not surprising that HNNs excel in prediction tasks. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether the computation of functional derivatives, a fundamental aspect of Hamiltonian Dynamics, is actually learned by HNNs. Our investigation into this inquiry leads us to an unexpected finding: HNNs are only able to accurately calculate their own derivatives when they are trained in a manner that utilizes Hamiltonian Dynamics. This discovery has significant implications for our understanding of how HNNs function and may also provide valuable insights for further research in the field.

Simply expanding a dataset through existing data does not guarantee an improvement in machine learning model performance or trustworthiness. To efficiently tackle this challenge, we suggest a collaborative approach where a team of experts and mathematicians models the behavior of existing data and assess the characteristics of new data. We develop a system of equations that represents how experts trust the predictions of machine learning models and new data. We also create a method for updating the system equations based on the outcomes of predictions and new data additions. We test this system through a simulated dataset and find that it is effective in increasing the performance and trustworthiness of machine learning models.

In x-ray based prohibited item detection, identifying items in real x-ray images is a challenging task due to the diversity of items and varying image quality. This complexity is compounded by the need to accurately classify items as prohibited or not. To address this issue in a real-world setting, we introduce a novel approach featuring a unique module that leverages residual learning to enhance low-frequency item information in x-ray images. This approach allows for the simultaneous detection and classification of items. We also present a large-scale high-quality benchmark called RexRay, comprising 130,000 training images and 11,000 test images with items labeled as prohibited or not, across eight categories. Comprehensive experiments have shown that our method outperforms existing architectures, achieving a high overall accuracy rate of 93.17% on the RexRay benchmark. Notably, our method excels in detecting small items and low-contrast items, which is crucial in real-world scenarios.

We introduce a novel, integrated quantum invariant called $V_L(q)$ for links in a thickened torus, derived from a combination of the Kauffman bracket skein module and a system of bar invariant polynomials. The construction of $V_L(q)$ draws inspiration from the volume hypothesis of the quantum invariant, specifically in its application to torus links. A key characteristic of $V_L(q)$ is its responsiveness to mutations of links, resulting in the outcome $V_L(q) = qV_{\mu(L)}(q^{-1})$. Moreover, this integrated invariant exhibits volume hypothesis behavior for certain links, namely those consisting of twisted torus links, and displays a geometric structure that can be viewed as a refinement of the volume hypothesis. Furthermore, $V_L(q)$ is an invariant of the link's complement, and has been extended to a broader class of objects, including knots and pseudo-links in $T^2 \times I$.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, particularly with the introduction of BERT, have led to significant progress in this area due to their ability to embed languages in a high-dimensional space, where words with the same sense are closer together.  Nonetheless, numerous challenges still persist in tackling this issue, notably dealing with limited training data, a lack of labeled data, and the contextual nature of word meanings.  To address these issues, this paper introduces Context-gloss Enhanced for WSD, a novel approach that utilizes a variety of contextual information to create a more comprehensive understanding of a word's meaning.  Our method leverages a vast, publicly accessible corpus to generate a wide range of relevant context for each word sense and builds upon this by incorporating a set of pre-trained language models.  Extensive experiments conducted on three distinct datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing the performance of WSD.

This paper formulates a conventional integral representation of the reciprocal gamma function in a context involving generalized functions and hyperspaces, also adapting a method to obtain a modified integral expression.

This letter explains the strategy for detecting top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions using the ATLAS and CMS detectors at the LHC, as well as the sensitivity of the searches to certain beyond-SM scenarios. Given the difficulty in directly observing top quark pairs through their full decay chain, our analysis focuses on the analysis of the associated production of top quarks with other particles, such as W bosons or the Higgs boson, which can be more easily detected due to higher energy thresholds and distinctive decay signatures. As a result, our discussion on detector performance and simulation assumes the presence of these associated production processes, which are also used as benchmarks for interpreting data in searches for new physics. Furthermore, we provide an overview of the beyond-SM scenarios that can lead to observable effects in top quark production, including those involving new scalar or vector particles that can cause flavor changing neutral currents or decay the top quark to lighter particles, and discuss the distinctive features of these scenarios that can be inferred from top quark observations in proton-nucleus collisions, which complement other available information and will be crucial in accurate interpretation of data in future analyses.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL translation: semantic interpretation and semantic generation. We are considering a cross-domain setting, where the system must understand and translate real-world language into structured SQL code across different domains. Notably, the input text often contains unnecessary information that must be disregarded during interpretation. Our research proposes an end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic interpretation model that removes unnecessary information by using a semantic matcher as an auxiliary task. This auxiliary task includes implicit and explicit matching components, which leverage a pre-trained neural language model to compare the meaning of natural language and improve the model's ability to interpret semantic structures. By incorporating a type-state graph and using a neural program execution model, our model can generate accurate and working SQL code. We have successfully applied our model to the Spider cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark and achieved the highest achievement rates in domain adaptation and few-shot learning settings.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy in relation to network-based data. It outlines the challenges and frameworks applicable to this area, including various private sharing protocols and machine learning methods. Furthermore, it discusses the critical issues of data efficiency and efficiency in relation to network-based data, and presents key findings from previous studies in this context. Additionally, the paper highlights the promising research directions and notable open problems in this field.

The vast amount of astronomical data to be collected by Euclid in the coming years will significantly impact various research fields, including cosmology, planet hunting, and star classification. To handle this wealth of information, it's imperative that the underlying systems and methods be thoroughly examined for limitations and potential areas of improvement. Here, we'll discuss the technical aspects of Euclid's data processing and reduction techniques and explain how these will be implemented across its two primary instruments, the Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer. Furthermore, we'll outline the tasks involved in releasing the raw and processed data to the scientific community and the heritage science prospects this presents.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a desired path and calculating the optimal distance between lanes, we can produce a variety of challenging network configurations. Our approach allows us to regulate the complexity of these configurations by controlling the curvature and sharp angles within the paths. Additionally, we can apply these road templates in three-dimensional scenarios, further expanding our testing capabilities.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. A novel application, music captioning, aims to enhance user experience on audio platforms by describing playlists. This new domain draws from both natural language processing and music information retrieval. Although relevant techniques have been developed, there is no established method for music captioning. In this paper, we introduce a model that combines a pre-trained neural language model with a neural Collaborative Filtering component, which we evaluate on a dataset featuring album descriptions. Our results demonstrate that the combined model outperforms both individual models and a baseline, while also offering the advantage of being straightforward to integrate with existing music recommendation systems.

Researchers have recently used quantum hydrodynamics to model the behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates and other interacting gases by incorporating the effects of quantum fluctuations.  In this work, we've developed a random quantum hydrodynamics approach for describing these systems in phase space.  This method involves setting up a system of nonlinear partial differential equations and has the benefit of being easily applicable to composite systems formed by intermingled Bose-Einstein condensates and populations governed by the Balazs-Lax formula.  We've demonstrated that our approach accurately reproduces previous quantum hydrodynamics results and predicts new quasi-hydrodynamics modes in system phase-space regions where both matter and energy coexist.  We anticipate that this new framework will provide valuable insights into the non-equilibrium behavior of interacting gases and will have a tangible impact in the field of quantum hydrodynamics.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address these issues, we present a novel approach called DCAN, which generates high-quality action proposals through two contexts: a primary context that produces proposals based on initial detection and a secondary context that refines and aggregates proposals through iterative grouping methods. By seamlessly integrating these two contexts, DCAN effectively balances the exploration of action variants while maintaining semantic distinctness. In addition to achieving state-of-the-art performance on the ActivityNet v1.3 benchmark, we also demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by achieving significant improvements on the challenging ActivityNet v1.0 dataset.

The Palm Tree Mode (PTM) remains an unsolved puzzle in the field of plasma physics, characterized by an ELM-like crash accompanied by an island chain in a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field field line direction. This study focuses on the impact of a newly discovered edge current on PTMs in the JET tokamak, utilizing both practical and numerical approaches. It discovered that a previously overlooked edge current, generated by a specific magnetic field configuration, plays a crucial role in the formation of an MHD island in a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. It was found that this edge current can cause a significant increase in the stability barrier height, resulting in an island in an unexpected direction. A numerical model incorporating this edge current in the VMEC code successfully reproduces the observed PTM phenomena in JET discharges. It was also discovered that this edge current can be managed through proper adjustment of the lower saddle location in quiescent H-mode plasmas, enabling the regeneration of the stable state required for PTMs.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for mobile robots working together in a shared environment. It introduces a novel approach that leverages dynamic vortex potential fields to prevent their movement from intersecting. The vortex potential fields are dynamic because they shift in response to changes in the robots' positions and movements. It has been mathematically proven that this method ensures collision-free coexistence and the development of the technique is illustrated through simulation and practical applications.

Consider a long sequence of letters where the position of each letter is associated with a random symbol from a set, essentially behaving as a random process over time. Given that the symbols at adjacent positions are not independent, we can still establish a large deviation principle for the frequency of specific co-occurring patterns within this stochastic process. This result applies to both independent and stationary processes, enabling us to derive a large deviation principle for the frequency of Markovian renewal processes as well.

A recent trend in wireless research is focused on utilizing Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRSs) to enhance system performance, particularly in the area of communication systems. To explore the potential of IRSs in radar systems, this paper investigates how an IRS can amplify a target's reflection signal, improving the accuracy of radar parameter estimation. A basic model is established and evaluated through simulations, with results showing that with the optimal placement of the IRS, radar parameter estimation can be more accurate and requires lower signal power. Furthermore, this study finds that by optimizing the reflection pattern of the IRS, even with a poorly placed IRS, radar parameter estimation can be more reliable and target detectability can be improved.

Fuzzers are widely used testing tools that help identify software vulnerabilities.
They operate by randomly modifying application inputs, then checking if the program
crashes, often providing valuable information on error causes.
Despite their effectiveness, traditional fuzzers have significant limitations, mainly
due to their slow testing speed and the fact that they require extensive time to
deliver results.
These challenges have prompted the development of new techniques, such as evolutionary
fuzzing and hybrid methods, which aim to enhance testing speed and efficiency.
Evolutionary fuzzing, in particular, utilizes algorithms inspired by natural selection
to create optimized inputs for triggering program crashes or specific behaviors.
These techniques typically involve complex evaluation functions that assess input
efficacy and often incorporate black-box and gray-box approaches to monitor application
behavior during testing.
One key aspect of these techniques is understanding how they compare to each other,
as well as to traditional and alternative methods of testing and validation.
This comparison is the focus of this work, which explores the strengths and weaknesses
of different testing methodologies, examines their practical applications, and
investigates potential areas for collaboration and integration.

Pretrained models have been integral in improving the performance of few-shot continuous learning on large-scale datasets. Notably, a 2020 study achieved remarkable results by using a frozen base model for continuous learning on the Colored MNIST, FMIST, and a combination of these datasets. We sought to investigate the underlying reasons for these successful outcomes. By replicating the mentioned results and extending the evaluation to additional benchmarks, we discovered that the successful applications of frozen pretrained models in continuous learning are subject to specific protocol limitations. Our analysis indicated that the difference in performance is primarily attributed to the inherent disparity between the training and testing protocols, and not necessarily the effectiveness of frozen pretrained models in continuous learning. We believe that these findings will serve as a pivotal starting point for the ongoing discussion aimed at clarifying the role of pretrained models in continuous learning.

We define a new concept of subdomains within a metric space, which we call 'C1,1-domains'. These subdomains possess characteristics similar to those of Lipschitz domains, while also allowing for the extension of classical results regarding one-dimensional minimal surfaces to higher-dimensional surfaces. Specifically, we prove that any minimal surface within a C1,1-domain can be assigned a topological invariant, which is determined by the surface's boundary and the domain's structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if two minimal surfaces share the same boundary and possess the same topological properties, then there exists a correspondence that maps one surface to the other. This correspondence is expressed in terms of the action of a group, which consists of combinations of reflections and translations.

This final installment concludes our in-depth analysis of the solutions $u$ to the given one-sided parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have distinct limits at positive and negative infinity, were previously examined in the earlier parts of the study. It was found that the solution $u$ exhibits distinct behavior based on whether the equation is reaction-diffusion or dissipative. If the equation is reaction-diffusion and has convergent, stable limits at positive and negative infinity, then the solution $u$ converges to the equilibrium solution connecting the two limit values. If, on the other hand, the equation is reaction-diffusion but the limits at positive and negative infinity are unstable, then the solution $u$ fails to converge to an equilibrium solution connecting the two limit values. Similarly, in the dissipative case, if the limits at positive and negative infinity are stable, then the solution $u$ converges to the equilibrium solution connecting the two limit values, whereas if the limits at positive and negative infinity are unstable, then the solution $u$ fails to converge to an equilibrium solution connecting the two limit values. This part of the study addresses the scenario where the equation is reaction-diffusion and the limits at positive and negative infinity are unstable. It was previously demonstrated in the earlier parts of the study that if the initial data have distinct limits at positive and negative

Recent experimental findings in 64Ni, specifically involving the 0+ states below 4.5 MeV, have been investigated. The aim is to clarify the presence of shape coexistence in this region through a monopole interaction within the valence shell. Calculations using the configuration interaction approach, with a monopole interaction tuned to mimic the effects of the 1d and 0s pairing forces, have been performed for 64Ni and its neighboring nickel isotopes. The results indicate that in 64Ni, protons and neutrons occupy equivalent shell spaces, and a specific pairing interaction causes them to separate into distinct groups, resulting in mixed configurations that produce low-lying 0+ and 2+ excited states characteristic of shape coexistence.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a class of games known as Lipschitz games, which are quite diverse and contain significant subclasses including constant games and those with bounded payoff. These games have the property that every equilibrium strategy can be achieved with a limited number of private randomizations of the players' actions. In our research, we establish a quantitative lower bound for the first type of complexity, with the specific result being that there are Lipschitz games requiring an exponentially large (in terms of beta) number of private randomizations to achieve some equilibrium. This result also implies the existence of games that necessitate an intricately complex endogenous complexity of at least polynomially many private randomizations to reach some approximate equilibrium of average quality. These findings contribute to our understanding of the query complexity of approximate equilibria in the broader category of lipshitz games.

Machine learning models are notoriously difficult to tune, and much research addresses this challenge through methods like efficient search algorithms. Another approach, less discussed but effective, is using users' prior knowledge about model performance via knowledge valves in an interactive framework. This paper introduces a different strategy, focusing on an unsupervised validation strategy where only a subset of the data is used for model evaluation. We explore this approach's effect on model selection and training in several experiments featuring standard datasets for NLP tasks. The results show that this strategy significantly reduces the variance of model performance metrics, making it easier to compare models and select the best one, even when the performance curves are highly irregular. Although this validation strategy may increase the risk of overfitting, we find that this is generally not a significant issue in our experiments. We conclude that this approach is a viable and effective way to tackle the tuning variance issue in NLP models.

Recently, Neural Network-based techniques have excelled in multiple tasks by establishing a knowledge learning foundation, where a knowledge-known neural network efficiently trains other neural networks. Despite significant progress, several issues remain in developing neural network training architectures, such as slow learning rates, difficulty in parallelization, and poor knowledge transfer capabilities. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of various neural network training architectures, discussing their key features and the techniques used to enhance the knowledge learning process. We also explore the challenges faced in parallel and distributed learning, as well as the potential applications of these architectures in collaborative knowledge learning.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of algorithms. Our method has the benefit of being more environmentally friendly as it uses significantly less memory space compared to traditional approaches. We have successfully applied our framework to develop a set of new algorithms that can solve complex Minimum Product Erasure (MPE) and constrained MPE problems exactly, outperforming existing exact methods while requiring substantially less memory. Our evaluation of this method on several real-world MPE datasets reveals a notable boost in computational speed and memory efficiency.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfer resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate key aspects of light-matter interaction, including momentum transfer, and these phenomena can be analyzed through a modification of the optical Bloch equations.

When subjected to high stresses, the viscosity of certain suspensions surge exponentially, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. This massive increase in viscosity is seen in a range of granular and molecular materials. Researchers propose that shear thickening serves as a stability indicator for complex systems, highlighting the need to thoroughly examine its underlying causes and scaling characteristics. Through precise measurements of the shear stress and viscosity during failure and steady-state conditions, researchers have identified the scaling of shear stress with the size of particles in multiple systems, providing a universal rule that can be used as a guide for navigating the physics of complex systems.

We introduce a new algebraic concept called the Racah algebra, which is a refinement of the Racah polynomial originally discovered by Terras. The Racah algebra leads to the development of the centralizer algebra $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, and its representation through the Hilbert-Poincaré series. These new structures provide a more fundamental explanation for the existence of the Racah polynomials, and they also offer intriguing connections to other areas such as pre-Schroeder operators, and a specialized case of the Solomon-Tits algebra.

Our study shows that in a bilayer hexagonal magnetic material, particularly in ${\rm Cu}_2{\rm O}_2{\rm Cl}_2$ with spin $1/2$, a proximity of exchange interactions in the two layers can result in the occurrence of a twisted superfluid or supersolid state, characterized by triplon condensation and multi-lattice coordination. The interlayer interaction must be near balance for this phenomenon to happen. This situation can be experimentally identified by analyzing the heat capacity and NMR relaxation rate in the ground state. Notably, this finding provides a theoretical basis for predicting the existence of a twisted superfluid or supersolid state in quantum magnetics.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-nucleus collision events. We initially developed a numerical method to simulate 3D scattering incidents, and utilized this method to examine the distribution of incident velocities and recoil angles resulting from such collisions. Additionally, we were able to derive an analytical formula for the spectral density of recoil energies in 3D scenarios, which aligns with existing 1D theories at low energy levels and differs from them at higher energy levels due to the anisotropic nature of 3D scattering incidents.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines how Web search personalisation influences knowledge work by assessing the visibility of relevant online information. The findings indicate that Web search personalisation can lead to a significant decrease (up to 70%) in the visibility of relevant online information, thereby significantly impacting professional knowledge work on the Web. In addition, the data reveals a notable disparity in search engine results between those displayed to professionals and those displayed to the general public, a discrepancy that has not been given sufficient attention in studies on Web search personalisation.

We are presenting a design for a cutting-edge particle collider that could revolutionize our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. This proposed facility, dubbed the $\mu$cooltron, has the potential to Smith and others' long-held dreams of accurately measuring the top quark's mass and the Higgs boson's couplings with heavy flavor. By doing so, it would significantly advance our knowledge of the underlying laws of physics. With its advanced tevatron-like design and sophisticated detector system, the $\mu$cooltron is capable of delivering groundbreaking results in several key areas, including searches for extra dimensions, Supersymmetry, and heavy gauge boson precision studies. Furthermore, it provides a platform for pioneering sciences such as dark matter and neutrino research. By leveraging its powerful capabilities, the $\mu$cooltron offers a comprehensive and ambitious research agenda that could greatly impact our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and light.

A novel approach is proposed to create high-quality, motion-free 4D T2-weighted MRI images from the average of continuously acquired 2D TSE images, using a data-driven residual learning residual network. The proposed framework bypasses the need for individual subject-specific motion correction techniques, leveraging a general respiratory motion correction map trained on a diverse group of subjects. The framework's ability to extend beyond 4D body imaging is made possible by integrating a data-driven residual learning residual network, which eliminates the requirement for spatial transformation. The proposed technique was compared to a conventional 4D MRI approach using clinically relevant imaging parameters and a phantom model, showing a notable reduction in motion artifacts and improved image quality. Additionally, the technique demonstrated comparable SNR to 4D MRI but with significantly shorter acquisition times.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to creating secure control systems for complex nonlinear processes subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Control Barrier Function (CBF) that can help prevent a system from entering hazardous states, even when faced with uncertain and malicious inputs, and provides an efficient and secure gradient-based algorithm for implementing the CBF subject to input constraints. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this control method through simulation tests on a nonlinear helicopter system.

In the course of modeling real-life phenomena, approximate comparisons based on a comparison function play a key role. This work builds upon the concept of comparison functions and introduces the idea of a continuous function approximation, which serves as the foundation for a novel approach to geometric region representation. It then establishes a connection between this approach and the method of using piecewise comparison functions for region representation. Additionally, it introduces the notion of a CF-approximation space and explores its properties.

The paired-permutation test in Broken Stick Assembly (BSA) models assembles two random subsets of a sequence to evaluate whether two datasets' structural components are similar in distribution. This test has seen a substantial increase in use recently in the analysis of genomic data. Although widely adopted, there are concerns about the test's validity due to its low empirical type I error rate and seeming insulation to the effect of increasing cluster sizes. We demonstrate that the traditional interpretation of type I error probability is inapplicable to paired-permutation tests in BSA models. Instead, the valid asymptotic distribution of the test statistic is multivariate normal with a reduced rank structure, mirroring the BSA model's dimensionality. We also introduce an accurate implementation of the test and provide empirical evidence to support its precision in comparison to the original paired-permutation test.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously studied topics within the shipping industry sector has been re-examined using this unified dataset, and additional research opportunities have been identified. Specifically, the data offers insights into the shipping industry's response to global economic fluctuations, as well as the complex relationships between shipping quantity and freight rate. Additionally, an investigation into the pricing behavior of new and used ships has revealed significant price disparities, as well as the results of Bayesian structural time series models, which have been applied to the data to identify hidden trends and seasonal patterns.

We define loom areas as a broader context for loom spaces in the veering tree of a translation generalizing this concept to a combinatorial framework. Our research demonstrates that the 1-skeleton of the loom area corresponds to the veering triangulation, and we further establish a topological equivalence between the loom area and the veering triangulation, including their respective boundary spaces.

Current graph neural networks (GNNs) mostly lack a clear interpretation of their internal workings due to their complex nature. To address this, we propose a novel approach called learned sparsification, which involves expressing specific GNN layers as elementary matrix multiplications and applying a factorization technique to these layers. This results in a simplified, easily interpretable representation of the network. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through a practical application, including an experiment showing that learned sparsification is effective in reducing the memory requirements of GNNs.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, there has been a concern that CountSketch might not be robust in settings where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous sketches. In a recent study, we demonstrate that CountSketch's performance does not significantly decline in adaptive input settings for many fundamental objects commonly analyzed in high-dimensional geometry. In such scenarios, the time and sampling size requirements for achieving desired accuracy can be shown to scale polynomially with the key parameter log(k), where k represents the number of top elements to be identified. Furthermore, we also establish lower bounds demonstrating that CountSketch's performance degrades at a rate of at least poly(log(k)) when dealing with adaptive inputs, thereby narrowing the gap in our upper bound result.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas with conformal infinity forming a product of a compact manifold and a tree, and satisfying certain standards, can be conformally deformed to a smooth, compact manifold if a specific condition is met. This condition involves the conformal action of the tree on the compact manifold being complete. In Part II, we demonstrate that the singular areas themselves can be smoothly deformed to a compact manifold under the same conformal structure, provided that the conformal action of the tree on the compact manifold is locally complete. This achievement is based on innovative techniques that include conformal capacity theory and geometric measure theory.

A critical reexamination of the Nernst effect in vortex liquids near the critical temperature is conducted, and a previous proposed link to the viscosity and mobile entropy in these systems is confirmed and further analyzed. It is demonstrated that the positive and negative components of the Nernst effect have distinct temporal relaxation times, which are directly related to the vortex dynamics. Based on the established connection between the Nernst effect and vortex dynamics, previous data on the positive component of the Nernst effect is reinterpreted, and it is shown that it is a direct measure of the vortex liquid's entropy associated with the movement of the vortex system. It is also shown that the absolute value of the positive component of the Nernst effect is greater than the entropy of the vortex liquid alone, and this additional entropy is attributed to the shear viscosity of the vortex system. A comparison between the shear viscosity of the vortex liquid and the shear viscosity of the normal metal tunnel barrier in a Josephson junction is made, and it is observed that the former is significantly greater than the latter. Furthermore, the ratio of the entropy of the vortex liquid to its viscosity is independent of the temperature and is equal to the critical magnetic field of the vortex lattice. It is also found that the ratio of the entropy of the vortex system to its viscosity is directly proportional to the square of the electron mean free path.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on an accurate understanding of their flexibility, which can be challenging to measure on a large scale. A novel approach is proposed that leverages real-time data and machine learning algorithms to efficiently estimate the aggregate flexibility of a group of loads in near real-time, thus enabling the integration of these loads into dynamic demand response systems. The proposed framework involves a learning component that adapts to changing consumer habits and incorporates uncertainty into its predictions, ensuring reliable results. Furthermore, the framework integrates with model predictive control through a linear approximation, thus enabling the management of complex state variables and making the approach suitable for large-scale systems. The results of the study demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, and its potential to handle a broad range of controllable loads with diverse characteristics.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock values. It starts with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock price based on technical indicators, global stock indexes, commodity prices, and historical prices along with the sentiment scores. This model's performance is compared to benchmark models including LSTM, GRU, vanilla GAN, and ARIMA.

We introduce a groundbreaking new approach to studying molecular envelopes around massive star-forming regions using a universal formalism. By leveraging a universal power-law density profile and a rigorous statistical analysis, we develop a method to examine the physical properties of these envelopes through the scattering of continuum and line spectra. This method enables a direct measurement of key envelope parameters, including mass-to-gas ratio, temperature, and density. By applying this framework to a sample of 11 high-mass star-forming regions observed with the Submillimeter Array, we develop an envelope model that accurately fits the observed data and reliably assesses the uncertainty of physical property calculations. The resulting analysis of continuum spectra and molecular line diagnostics provides valuable insights into the physics and chemistry of massive star-forming regions, and our study of spectral features resolves underlying processes affecting the scattering of spectra. Furthermore, our examination of the variability of line ratios and continuum spectra across our sample and with external comparisons reveals significant variations that offer a deeper understanding of the complex nature and possible evolution of these regions.

This research investigates the capabilities of future TeV $e^+e^-$ colliders to
study double Higgs boson production within the context of the Standard Model and its variants, with a particular focus on certain types of Beyond-Standard-Model Higgs interactions. By employing Effective Field Theory and integrating Higgs effective operators into the theoretical framework, we calculated the double Higgs production process in the $e^+e^-\to ZHH$ and $e^+e^-\to HHH$ channels and analyzed their relevant observables, including Higgs invariant masses, beam thrust, and double differential distributions in Higgs invariant masses. Our analysis was performed for an 380 TeV and 350 TeV lepton colliders, with 5 ab$^{-1}$ and 10 ab$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, respectively. We used these analyses to investigate the double Higgs production process's sensitivity to various BSM Higgs interactions, with couplings that deviate from Standard Model predictions, and considered scenarios where certain Higgs interactions are modified while others remain standard. We also examined BSM interactions that change the Higgs self-coupling and the Standard Model's self-interaction constant, and found that future TeV $e^+e-$ colliders have the capability to investigate BSM interactions at a level of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})$ or lower, given that the BSM sector's BSM scale is higher than the

The recent discovery of gravitational waves by LIGO and VIRGO has allowed for the advancement of metric gravity theories through the detection of several multi-dimensional parameters. Although these breakthroughs have significantly improved metric gravity theories, the lack of observable effects at a microscopic scale in these theories remains. In contrast, the development of Lagrangian density formulations for metric gravity theories has been slow. In this paper, a comprehensive Lagrangian density has been created for a specific class of metric gravity theories, known as $f(T, B)$ gravity, where $T$ represents the torsion tensor and $B$ represents the batch tensor. This comprehensive Lagrangian density includes a term that is invariant to coordinate transformations and yields a feasible and observable signature for certain four-dimensional metrics. In addition, the paper presents a metric gravity field equation derived from the comprehensive Lagrangian density formulated in the metric affine gravity framework. Furthermore, the paper also explores the possibility of non-cinetic gravity, where the covariant divergence of the contortion tensor is zero, resulting in the simplification of the field equation to a purely harmonic condition.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It's discovered that a basic set of ordinary differential equations can accurately determine the behavior of shocks at localized areas, especially when those shocks form a 45-degree angle. A series expansion technique is utilized to further increase the speed of computations, resulting in significant improvements for shocks with larger gradients. A crucial new property is found for all localized shocks, confirming a long-standing prediction first made by holographic theory, and their behavior is closely studied at early and late stages of the collision. A key set of non-linear equations is derived that controls the behavior of the endpoint of the collision, and it's discovered that a critical new mode emerges that wasn't present in previous analyses, largely due to the presence of linearized perturbations. A key set of non-linear equations is also derived that controls the behavior of the endpoint of the collision for a specific important mode, and it's discovered that a critical new mode emerges that wasn't present in previous analyses, and it's behavior is closely studied at very short and very long times.

We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a granular medium, specifically a spherical cylinder, and interestingly found that its drag varies based on the angle of incidence. This anisotropic behavior was observed in both static and dynamic conditions of a surrounding fluid. Experiments using a high-speed camera and EMD (electromagnetic flow meter) to measure force were conducted for dry and water-saturated states of the granular bed. Analysis of the data revealed a significant increase in drag when the cylinder moves perpendicular to its long axis, and interestingly this anisotropic effect is more pronounced when it moves quickly. Additionally, drag force was found to be influenced by both the speed of the cylinder and the depth of the granular bed, with larger beds resulting in larger forces due to increased friction at the interface. This research provides valuable insights into the interaction between cylindrical objects and granular fluids, and has implications for a broader range of applications involving flow through saturated beds, and the behavior of cylindrical particles in these environments.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit to which outflows can continue over time. Our findings are consistent with a self-regulating feedback loop powered by outflows, where the mass ejected by outflows is greater than the mass converted into new stars, primarily through a process where gas is channeled back into the central regions of the galaxy.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for complex systems face challenges when dealing with a large number of parameters. Despite recent advancements in transfer learning and meta-learning, a novel approach is introduced that leverages a systematic organization of parameter interactions, enabled by Graph Neural Networks, into a directed acyclic graph. This approach allows for efficient evaluation of the tuning space, reducing the necessary evaluations by a factor of 10 to 100 while achieving a similar or better auto-tuned performance. A demonstration of the technique is provided through its application to the tuning of a cloud database system, showcasing its effectiveness.

Our research investigates the triangular flow's origin within a multiphase transport model, where we examine both the initial conditions and the interactions between particles during the medium's evolution. We discovered that the triangular flow's magnitude is influenced by the angle $\Delta\phi$ in a minimum-bias sense and that it differs based on whether it's associated with a same-side or opposite-side flow component. Additionally, we found that the initial anisotropic distribution of particles plays a significant role in creating the triangular flow. Furthermore, we observed that the triangular flow becomes more pronounced when the medium's interaction length increases, which supports the idea that it is linked to the triangular correlation between particles.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has been rising substantially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine access and interconnection.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, preventing effective retrieval and subsequent analysis.  Currently, there is a lack of methods for comprehensively evaluating the quality of RDF datasets, a domain that this paper seeks to address through an innovative, scalable framework.  This framework is an adaptation of the Apache Jena framework for creating and managing RDF datasets and includes novel techniques for quality assessment, specifically tailored for large-scale datasets and powered by a robust set of quality metrics carefully selected to cater to the nuances of RDF and Linked Data.  A novel score system and a cutting-edge technique for quality evaluation were also introduced, allowing for a score for each individual data point as well as an overall quality score for the entire dataset.  The effectiveness of this framework was validated through a series of large-scale and medium-scale use cases, and it is available for public access through the Data Quality Evaluation (DQE) framework at https://github.com/sameerchandel/dqe.

When working with complex stochastic processes, the MCMC method is often employed for its ability to handle non-Gaussian distributions and non-linear relationships. However, when observing these processes at irregular time points, a significant issue arises regarding the system parameter estimation. A novel approach is proposed in this study to estimate parameters in discrete data sets based on the sampling equation. The proposed method's efficiency and accuracy are validated through numerical experiments conducted on simulated data sets. Furthermore, the proposed approach is applied to real-world data analyzing the disappearance rate of the Yangtze river dolphin and the stability of the African elephant population.

We analyzed 1,000 lines of gas emission, spanning temperatures of 10,000 to 10 million Kelvin, in the centers of 13 Seyfert galaxies using high-quality integral field spectroscopy data. These observations were part of the CALIFA and MaNGA spectroscopic surveys. Our analysis used 3D spectroscopy and radiative hydrodynamics simulations to study the gas emission outside the axis of highest ionization, a phenomenon observed in the very hot OIII lambda 5007 line. Our results showed a significant increase in this emission's equivalent width at higher galactic masses, luminosities, and distances from the active galactic nucleus. We interpreted these findings as signs of gas excited by the active galactic nucleus being affected by its outflow. Additionally, we observed a significant increase in the OIII lambda 5007 to HeII lambda 4686 intensity ratio at higher ionization points, a phenomenon more commonly observed in quasars. This pattern was seen in all large galaxies but was absent in the smaller ones. These outcomes challenged existing theories of active galactic nucleus ionization that predict HeII lambda 4686 to be more intensely emitted than OIII lambda 5007 along the axis of highest ionization.

The growing number of mobile applications and the increasing sophistication of software are generating enormous amounts of event data, which, if properly harnessed, can significantly boost the performance of edge computing. Given the complex nature of these events, a new approach is required to effectively process and utilize the generated data, starting with a thorough understanding of events through description, their causes, and their effects. Towards this end, we present a novel framework that automates the analysis of events by identifying relevant information, pinpointing event sources, and forecasting future event occurrences, thereby enhancing the efficacy of edge computing.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider has collected an extensive dataset allowing for precise studies of rare and unusual phenomena in the interaction of beauty mesons with anti-muons, specifically CP violation and certain decay modes. With a proton energy of 8.16 TeV and a dataset of 80 inverse picobarns of data, the ATLAS collaboration has investigated several areas, including the violation of CP symmetry in the decay of neutral B mesons to muons and electrons, and the decay of charmless K mesons to various particles. The results represent the most up-to-date findings from the ATLAS collaboration to date.

The generation of realistic traffic scenes through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert vehicles randomly, yet lack the organization seen in actual scenes. In contrast, we propose SceneGen, an automated system that generates realistic traffic scenarios through understanding the underlying patterns of ordered vehicle placement. SceneGen is unique in its ability to create authentic traffic configurations from raw map data, unlike other approaches that utilize predefined maps. Through thorough evaluation using both synthetic and actual traffic data, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to produce highly realistic traffic scenes.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic states that are linked to subgroups of D_n, the symmetry group of the lattice, and these states are not attainable through a direct application of the FKG inequality.

A critical aspect in developing numerical methods for dynamic partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of creating and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including preserving a equation's energy, conservation of specific quantities, or boundary conditions. Although these discretization methods yield stable and physically realistic numerical solutions, they can suffer from low convergence rates, compounded by large starting errors in subsequent interpretation stages. To address this limitation, this study examines the application of preconditioned Krylov techniques to balance computational efficiency and preservation of the underlying solution's properties. Initial condition preservation, specifically, is the focus, along with a novel, structure-preserving implementation of the Conjugate Gradient method. The paper also supplies a framework for addressing other preservation-based problems. Experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of this approach, along with a discussion on potential avenues for further research, conclude the study.

A group of integers $a_n$ is considered ergodic with respect to a number $m$ if the sequence $m^na_n$ becomes periodic after some point $n_0$. If $m_1$ and $m_2$ are two relatively prime integers, then the combined ergodicity of the sequences $a_n$ with respect to $m_1$ and $m_2$ means that the sequence $m_1^{n_1}m_2^{n_2}a_n$ becomes periodic for some values $n_1, n_2 \geq 0$. It has already been established that there are infinitely many $a_n$ for which $\{2, 5\}$-combined ergodicity holds. This paper builds on that finding and demonstrates that there are infinitely many sequences satisfying $\{3, 4\}$-combined ergodicity.

We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust particle formation. Our goals were to
understand dust creation in low-metallicity environments and assess pair-
instability supernovae's role in superbubble evolution. Our simulations
revealed significant differences between models featuring pair-instability and
core-collapse supernovae in terms of gas temperature distribution and density
within the superbubble's outermost barionic region. In models including pair-
instability supernovae, temperatures above 0.1 eV were present at larger
radii, with more extensive cooling channels and increased dust formation rates
at radii where dense gas condenses into self-gravitating sheets. As a result,
more massive dust particles form in these situations, leading to increased dust
production in models including pair-instability supernovae by a factor of up
to ten in massive particles with growth exponents between -3.4 and -2.4. We
expect all pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae to contribute to dust
creation, with further increases possible in superbubble environments where
self-gravitating gas sheets form, such as in the 30 Doradus galaxy.

In this work, we introduce Far3Det, a novel 3D object detection task called far-field 3D detection. Unlike typical 3D detection tasks, which focus on objects within a relatively close range to the camera, far-field 3D detection aims to identify objects at farther distances. We establish a new benchmark for this task and propose a model called FarFieldRotor, which incorporates a innovative module called the FrontBackAxisRotator to address the significant challenges posed by Far3Det. The proposed model has achieved impressive performance on the newly introduced Far3Det benchmark, outperforming a basic 3D detection baseline by a considerable margin. Notably, our results suggest that there is a substantial performance gap between models optimized for near-field and those optimized for far-field 3D detection.

Chemical compounds are modeled as interacting fermions in a consistent framework, and we explore the potential of quantum machine learning to describe these systems' ground states. By training a quantum circuit network on the circuit ground state with a mean-field approximation, we achieve accurate descriptions of approximated ground states for both lattice models and real materials, leveraging the circuit state parity transformation to enforce fermionic anti-commutation relations. The simplicity of these descriptions enables fast evaluations of physical properties and efficient simulations of excited states and dynamics. The paradigm of quantum machine learning is not only applicable to traditional model systems but also adaptable to describing complex materials with band structures, effective for areas like materials design.

Soft-tissue motion during cardiac catheterization procedures introduces significant alignment challenges for medical imaging registration. This research addresses this issue by leveraging a physics-based model that takes into account the unique properties and behavior of blood vessels. The model simulates vessel dynamics and provides optimal mapping transformations. We've developed an iterative algorithm to effectively integrate the model-driven predictions with the available imaging data. The proposed method is suitable for large-scale deformations and has been successfully demonstrated on simulated and real-world data.

For a specific type of stationary and spherically symmetric spacetime, research has yielded conformal Killing vector fields on its extended manifold, including the conjugate manifold. The relationship between these fields and the energy-momentum tensor's conformal Killing vector fields in Einstein's general theory of relativity is examined, revealing their connection is determined by the energy-momentum tensor itself. This link, derived from the Einstein field equations, is a key factor in the development of conformal integrability in the context of gravitational physics. This research also implies that typical stationary, spherically symmetric spacetimes do not possess conformal Killing-Yano tensors, a finding that contrasts the outcomes of Gannon and Gurses, who found such tensors in the Schwarzschild and Robertson-Walker cases, with the exception of a specific conformally flat spacetime.

In this research, we are identifying the primary challenge in establishing correspondences for optical flow and scene flow. We believe that these correspondences should be based on a metric that is consistent, not just on the information provided by nearby pixels. We develop a metric learning method for self-supervised scene flow estimation that utilizes inconsistent correspondences as a warning sign. Our approach is to treat inconsistent correspondences as fake data and use a contrastive loss function to establish a reliable metric. We further refine this metric through a cross-frame correspondences loss function, which encourages consistent flows across frames. We employ this metric in a bi-directional flow estimation framework, which allows us to draw inspiration from the unique patterns in unidirectional flow fields. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised flow estimation techniques and achieves nearly identical performance to baseline flow estimation methods based on pre-trained models, with only a small increase in computational cost.

In recent years, AI networks, which are characterized by their biological inspiration and flexible operation between spiking and non-spiking modes, have been increasingly popular. Despite being similar to neural networks in structure, they differ in their computation method, offering improved energy efficiency and a more natural framework for mimicking living neural systems. One type of this network, known as the Random Neural Network (RNN), has previously been proposed but has exhibited poor classification precision when RNNs are used as multiple layers. To address this issue, this study introduces an enhanced RNN that uses a more advanced learning rule and incorporates a spike-time-dependent plasticity mechanism, allowing it to learn and classify data with greater precision at a lower energy cost. Moreover, the research finds that by switching to spiking mode during the classification phase, it achieves comparable classification precision to non-spiking networks while significantly reducing energy consumption. The findings are backed by experimental data, which shows that this new RNN offers improved precision and reduced energy consumption for both small and large datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, using the MIT bag model. We derived the pressure of spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field and at finite temperature, and subsequently, we determined the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field and at finite temperature. We then examined the relationship between the mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars and their radius, as well as the rotation period, in the presence of a strong magnetic field and at finite temperature.

In this study, we present a new, more compact characterization for a subset of cubic graphs that have perfect matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and odd edge-colourings. These specific cubic graphs are part of the broader category of cubic graphs with 3-regular 2-factors. Our analysis involves using a novel approach that involves determining the number of Hamiltonian cycles in a particular subgraph and showing its relationship to edge-colourings. Our findings essentially provide a non-trivial generalization of a previous theorem by Las Vergnas and Mohammadi.

We analyze block arrangements of lines to derive limitations on the possible GCDs of a specific set of combined polynomials. Specifically, we investigate whether there are instances where the GCD of a pair of polynomials exceeds a certain prime value, considering various factors such as the number of points used, the number of lines in each arrangement and whether the points are in general position. Our findings provide implications for the efficacy of certain algorithms used in computational geometry and geometric nullstellensatz proofs.

This paper introduces a new approach called Timeloops to efficiently manage system calls within containerized microservices by learning an autonomous policy. By examining the past behavior of system calls, a time-dependent call history pattern is identified, allowing for a natural extension into the future. Through testing, our research demonstrates that Timeloops is capable of balancing security and performance, outperforming existing solutions by significantly reducing unnecessary system calls and related latency.

Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. Within an augmented Standard Model, including a $B-L$ extension, we discover that the dark matter constellation can be comprised of pseudo-Goldstone bosons originating from a spontaneously broken $U(1)$ symmetry associated with the right-handed neutrinos' multiplet. The standard model gauge group can be gauged, allowing for a connection between the $B-L$ symmetry and the dark matter sector. The model's viability in the context of the Standard Model, including the stability of the vacuum, the dark matter constituency, and the model's predictability through the value of the dark photon mass, is thoroughly examined. The model also offers a natural mechanism for the creation of dark matter through the decay of the inert Higgs boson, and we derive the relevant LHC constraints. The model's viability at the Large Hadron Collider and direct dark matter detection experiments, such as XENON1T, will be extensively explored.

The probability mass function based multiple binary measurement filter (PMBM) has been a prominent method in tracking scenarios where multiple targets with different speeds are present. Unlike other methods, this filter maintains a detailed origin model, dividing the state space into evenly sized grids to calculate the probability of target existence. However, as the number of targets increases or their speed spans a wide range, grid size becomes impractically small, necessitating a different approach to dividing the origin space. Alternatively, the space could be divided in a non-uniform manner, adapted to the characteristics of the moving targets. This study proposes using such a grid in the PMBM filter, enabling it to handle complex target scenarios with reduced grid size, thereby improving computation efficiency. Moreover, this modification is particularly beneficial in sensor management systems, where energy is minimized by optimizing target tracking.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior decay term. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system valid only at a specific time interval and then deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a suitable control function for a given time frame. Additionally, we show that a more restrictive estimate, namely a weak Carleman estimate, can be employed to extend our initial result to a broader class of population models.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even minor mistakes made by players can have significant consequences, with opponents seizing on any error to counter-attack and turn the game's momentum in their favor. In such pivotal moments, a team's strategy shifts from possession to safety, with a focus on preventing goals and maintaining their position on the field. Through successful actions in these situations, a team can regain possession of the ball and resume their desired gameplay. With the extent of these moments increasing with higher league rankings, understanding and implementing optimal team behavior in these critical situations is crucial. We address this need by modeling these situations through a Markov Decision Process and solving them with Deep Reinforcement Learning, with our proposed approach allowing a virtual soccer team to adapt to changing game circumstances and prioritize goal prevention over scoring. In a collaborative multi-agent environment, our results show our approach outperforms traditional methods and achieves successful actions in critical game states.

High-resolution imaging in seismic exploration is typically achieved through integral imaging techniques such as migration. These methods reliably produce high-resolution images, albeit with limitations in accurately modeling real-world seismic phenomena. In contrast, advanced modeling techniques like extended source theory (XST) provide a more realistic representation of seismic events by extending the source along the recorded wavefield path. This work proposes a new framework called extended source wavefield reconstruction (XS-WFR) that mathematically connects XST to traditional wavefield reconstruction and migration methods. By applying this framework to simulated and real-world data sets, we observe a notable improvement in imaging accuracy, especially in areas with complex geological structures and where traditional methods fail. Therefore, we believe that XS-WFR has significant potential to further enhance the quality of seismic images.

In the realm of classical optics, optical systems with symmetry exhibit the same behavior regardless of the input polarization. This invariance is known as linear optical coherence. It has been largely maintained in quantum optics, where only certain types of entanglement, such as symmetric Gaussian states, can be coherently manipulated in balanced linear optical devices. Our research demonstrates that these restrictions can be released by introducing quantum squeezing in one of the output fields. This results in the creation of asymmetric linear optical states and their corresponding counterparts in quantum optics. The associated increases in linear optical coherence go beyond entanglement and include sub-lamb lineshapes in spectra and improved precision in interferometric measurements. The potential of these states is illustrated through the implementation of an interferometer, which demonstrates an increase in precision by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ when quantum squeezing is present.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray transient IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst. Timing and spectral data from the AstroSat were used to analyze a low-frequency Quasi Periodic Oscillation and a Cyclotron Line Feature, both of which were previously reported but in need of further confirmation and line energy estimation. Our analysis of the spectroscopic data from the AstroSat soft X-ray telescope (SXT) and the Astrosat Transient Sky Monitor (ASTROSAT TESS) during the 2019 outburst, yielded a QPO frequency of approximately 0.036 Hz and a Cyclotron Line Energy of around 42.7 keV, confirming earlier observations and providing new insights into the binary system's behavior.

To analyze the dynamics of species competition, an extension of the voter model was developed with the addition of birth and death processes. This 'elector model' can model competition and colonization processes, incorporating a key 'tradeoff' concept. The model was investigated in a quenched random environment, and results showed that a strong competition-colonization tradeoff can lead to the permanent exclusion of one species from coexistence equilibrium. Conversely, mild tradeoffs allow for permanent coexistence, while extremely strong tradeoffs can result in the dominance of one species over the other. The model also demonstrates the fragile nature of coexistence equilibrium, as a slight increase in the strength of competitive interactions can lead to the permanent exclusion of one species. These findings are confirmed through numerical simulations and the parameters of the model are analytically simplified to illustrate the exotic phenomenon of stable one species dominance through a strong competition-colonization tradeoff in random environments.

Historical sundials were a primary means of determining local time before the advent of mechanical clocks. This technology, dating back to ancient civilizations, used the shadow of a vertical object to indicate time. As the position of the sun changes, sundials display different shadow lengths, allowing users to estimate local time. In regions with known latitude, sundials can be effectively employed as timekeeping devices. We aim to document and analyze a collection of Indonesian sundials, focusing on those that incorporate Islamic architectural elements, to explore their potential as historical timekeepers and to make them freely accessible for educational purposes.

A Reflecting Surface-Aided Integrated Data and Energy Networking (RIS-AIDEN) framework is proposed to optimize an objective function that considers both cognitive capabilities and D2D communication interference. To tackle this non-convex problem, the system is first partitioned into independent sub-systems and an algorithm based on block coordinate descent is employed to obtain a local optimal solution. The RIS-AIDEN performance is evaluated through numerical simulations and shown to achieve significant improvements over traditional approaches, primarily due to the increased cognitive capabilities and reduced D2D communication interference.

This paper describes the setup and testing of a novel 2D measurement system using a single-point LDV system. By positioning the LDV system far from the test area and using a large-diameter lens, we can record the velocity data from which the x and y components of the velocity are derived. This method was successfully used in measuring the flow velocities in a model channel flow, as seen in the included results. Furthermore, this technique has been theoretically analyzed to determine its limitations and potential for applying it to various types of flow experiments.

The theory of electron microscopy suggests that spherical and chromatic aberrations have inherent limitations and cannot be fully mitigated, which has led to the development of sophisticated technologies such as monozonal lenses and multicomponent lenses to manage them. Programmable lens systems offer flexibility in adjusting lens settings, allowing for the optimization of image formation based on object characteristics. By reconfiguring the lens system, it's possible to selectively suppress central and side bands of the diffraction pattern, thus improving resolution and contrast. Notably, this approach surpasses the theoretical limits imposed by spherical and chromatic aberrations, resulting in enhanced performance without the need for complicated lens designs.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, research has also begun to examine the internal state of language models after processing the input and how it impacts the response generated. This work extends that research by investigating the relationship between the encoder representations of input data and the quality of the response generated. We discover that these encoder representations are often insufficiently informative, leading to subpar response generation, and identify particular challenges related to the diverse nature of dialogue and the difficulty of forecasting the next message. This study's findings may be seen as an extension to prior research on preconditions for coherent response generation, and we propose a possible remedy to this issue involving the incorporation of task-related information into the encoder through a learned switch that normalizes the internal state of the language model for the specific task at hand. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by conducting a series of experiments, and our evaluations suggest that it has the potential to enhance dialogue system performance.

A key challenge in autonomous off-road navigation using LiDAR sensors is the consistent localization of a vehicle within a previously mapped environment. This challenge stems from the diverse and ever-changing nature of off-road terrain, which renders traditional place recognition approaches ineffective. In this paper, we introduce a novel LiDAR-based place recognition framework, called AttDLNet, which leverages deep learning networks to extract both local and global contextual features from 3D point clouds. This framework includes a compact network that extracts local contextual features in the form of rotating 3D cylinders and a more complex global network for feature aggregation.
