Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive pregnancy checks and frequent screenings in high-risk patients due to ongoing emissions safety concerns.
Low-dose PET (LD-PET) images, while acceptable for tracking disease progression, do not provide accurate information needed for active treatment planning.
In this paper, we introduce an innovative uncertainty-aware neural network approach that integrates information from two sources – low-dose PET images and corresponding blood pool CT images – to produce high-quality PET images corresponding to the doses currently in use.
By leveraging the diversity of training data, our model excels in predicting outcomes for new, unseen low-dose PET images;
it does this by identifying and limiting its predictions to physically plausible values for the related quantities, thus enhancing the reliability of its outcomes. 
We compare our resiliant, uncertainty-aware neural network to traditional approaches by training and evaluating it on a large, real-world dataset of 3882 PET scans;
it demonstrates a notable improvement in the quality of the predicted images and their accuracy. 
In particular, it outperforms the baseline model in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 21, and achieves more accurate results as measured by the structural similarity index (SSIM), with a 13% increase. 
Also, our model significantly reduces the bias present in the predicted images, eliminating it by 88%. 
It is worth noting that while it outperforms traditional approaches, our model does

Personalization is ubiquitous in today's online platforms, which often employ sophisticated techniques to present users with tailored content. Although seemingly beneficial, this customization can be a threat to users' privacy. To explore this complex issue, we invite conference attendees to engage in a critical discussion, examining both positive and negative aspects of personalized experiences as they relate to privacy. We also offer thought-provoking questions to facilitate an exchange of ideas among conference participants and lay the groundwork for future research in this area.

A fundamental linguistic concept, centering theory, was introduced over two decades ago to improve our understanding of how people comprehend and deliver simple spoken messages. This paper aims to investigate the link between centering theory and coreference resolution, specifically using a current state-of-the-art coreference resolution model. We analyzed how this model's predictions align with coreference resolution data by categorizing mentions as central or non-central according to centering theory. Our findings indicate that coreference resolution errors tend to occur more frequently with non-central mentions. We subsequently developed new metrics to gauge the relationship between these mentions and the model's performance. These assessments reveal that both the baseline system and our augmented system tend to err more often with non-central mentions. We further examined mention types with distinct centering properties and discovered that coreference resolution errors are more common when mentions have similar centering scores or when they possess different centering levels.

We have devised parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we have found set-decompositions and tree-decompositions that enable us to determine in a finite number of steps whether a directed graph has an upward planar representation. Additionally, we have established that the problem of recognizing whether a directed graph can be laid out in an upward planar manner is solvable in a time that is polynomial relative to the size of the input, given a parameter that does not exceed a certain value. This certain value represents the maximum number of edges that are contained within any single subgraph of the directed graph.

The rising intricacy of modern computer systems demands elevated expertise and considerable time to set up, hindering user adoption and slowing down innovation pace. Automated setup processes are crucial for businesses to effectively leverage their resources and technology advancements. Unfortunately, existing automation approaches are largely centered around repetitive tasks, leaving complex setup processes unresolved. We propose a novel, widely-applicable framework that utilizes model checking and model transformation to automate setup processes efficiently. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a practical application involving the configuration of a Web services system.

The average growth of a system's operators can be measured by the commutator chain, exponential growth, or sublinear growth laws. This work connects these indicators by measuring the commutator widths and comparing them with the eigenvalues of specific Hamiltonians. We find that the average commutator width increases exponentially with the system size for both free-fermion and circulant-ensemble models, which have slow operator spreading. Conversely, systems with broad spreading, like the XXZ chain near its critical point, exhibit a commutator width that scales sublinearly with the system size. Moreover, we observe that the variance of the commutator width narrows as operator spreading accelerates in some cases. Our findings are further validated by numerical simulations of random Hamiltonians.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for indoor location detection, given its widespread availability and cost-effectiveness. In this technique, a device with a WiFi adapter is used to measure the signal strength of accessible access points, which is then correlated with the physical location of the device. Through supervised machine learning, we can enhance the accuracy of the estimation process. In this research, we compare the effectiveness of various algorithms, including K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and Neural Networks, in estimating the distance between devices and known locations within a room. The evaluation was conducted using a dataset collected from 11 different locations and 11 varying WiFi access points. The results show that Random Forest outperforms the other algorithms, yielding a mean absolute error of 1.5 meters. This demonstrates that, with sufficient training data, the error rate can be reduced to acceptable levels for a wide range of indoor applications.

We're investigating the optimal energy output of a large array of solar panels covering the surface of an event horizon, as a part of an artificial structure similar to a Dyson shell surrounding a black hole. This analysis aims to determine the maximum energy that could be generated by such a system, considering the extreme redshift of energy emitted from the event horizon due to its high curvature. Using the concept of complex Riemann surface, we derive a mathematical formula to calculate the optimal energy output as a fraction of the total energy emitted by the black hole, specifically for its electromagnetic, gravitational and kinetic components. Furthermore, we apply this formula to a black hole surrounded by matter and energy, as well as during its final stages of collapse into a black hole.

Network applications rely heavily on service quality, and issues arise when this quality isn't met as expected. The problem is identifying the source of these quality issues. To address this challenge, companies are investing in complex systems to detect and resolve SLA breaches. This paper explores using a peer-to-peer approach to tackle this challenge. We examine the underlying architecture, detailing a proposed system designed to detect and resolve SLA breaches and providing a basic implementation of this system. Key benefits of this approach include reduced costs, better security, and greater scalability, among others. We compare our method to traditional approaches and highlight future areas of research for this phenomenon.

The phenomenon of beam breakup (BBU) poses a significant threat to particle accelerators, particularly those used in energy recovery linacs (ERLs). BBU can induce oscillations in the beam, leading to a decline in the required electromagnetic field and ultimately limiting the achievable current. This study sheds light on an unforeseen factor influencing BBU in ERLs: the design of the filling pattern. Our experiments demonstrate that an unusual pattern results in a notable increase in the threshold current, often exceeding traditional estimates by more than ten times. This groundbreaking finding is attributed to the unique interaction between the beam and the filling pattern's harmonic fields. To further investigate this discovery, a related theoretical analysis is also presented.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems are necessary. One crucial factor these experiments need to account for is the total cross-section of neutrons with hydrogen, which involves a fundamental nuclear interaction that has not been thoroughly understood in the 0.1--100 GeV energy range. In this study, a 3D scintillator sensor with a novel projection technique was used to measure this cross-section with high precision at the J-PARC MLF, specifically at the neutron time-of-flight channel of the J-PARC neutron facility. Results showed a precision of 0.5--2% across various energy ranges, which has significant implications for the research of neutrino oscillations and long-baseline neutrino detection systems.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effects of surface moisture on these particles under various temperature conditions. In a laboratory setting mimicking conditions up to 1000 K, samples with different levels of water content were observed under scanning electron microscopes after being subjected to slow collisions. In all scenarios, sticking forces remained strong even at high temperatures due to the presence of water, which allows for a more thorough examination of how these particles interact with each other in a environment similar to that of a forming planetary system in the presence of intense parental star light. In such circumstances, particles with water on their surfaces maintain close proximity to each other even when tilted at high angles in flows resulting from gravitational forces, increasing the likelihood of them coming together and merging into even larger bodies.

This R package, lfda, is dedicated to executing local Fisher discriminant analysis on a given dataset. The method was initially proposed in Liang et al. (2019), allowing users to embed high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while retaining class information. The package also facilitates the visualization of embedded data and enables the creation of 3D plots using the plotly package. Furthermore, lfda is adaptable to handling imbalanced multiclass problems.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various challenges including high-dimensional state spaces, complex reward functions, and non-linear obstacles, but have yet to fully address all of these difficulties in a single framework. This paper presents a novel strategy, referred to as EKMP, for learning from human demonstrations in complex, real-world settings, characterized by complex reward functions, high-dimensional state spaces, and challenging constraints that cannot be linearized. We provide a practical algorithm and evaluate its effectiveness through the transfer of human skills to a difficult kitchen navigation task, involving multiple moving obstacles. The results of our experiments highlight the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art imitation learning algorithms, revealing an average success rate of 80% in task transfer, significantly outperforming the 20% achievement of the next best method.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this paper, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory is calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation is constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

A novel topological superfluidity characterized by spin-polarized and fermionic-liquid states has been identified in a Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions, located at its Fermi surface's intersection point. Corresponding quasi-particle residues were found to be very small, indicating that this exotic matter state is highly unstable and prone to fragmentation into two separate topological superfluid components, each with spin singlet characteristics. Additionally, in the model's mean-field Rashba strong-coupling regime, a $p$-orbital paired superfluid state with zero spin polarization and a fermionic liquid state separated by a gap have been discovered, both displaying topological properties.

By using small-angle neutron scattering and X-ray diffraction, we detected a sudden change in the arrangement of interlocked vortices as temperature decreases through a critical point near 6.4 K in optimally doped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. This transition isn't associated with an anomaly at the vortex core and may be triggered by an increased effectiveness of vortex-core disorder on the Luther-Emery liquid. This finding could have a significant impact on theories of competing orders in cuprates.

Theories predicting highly extended polymer brush behavior have been developed, yet they often lack precision and have not been directly observed in experiments. Recent studies using scanning force microscopy on cross-linked polymer brushes confirm that alternative theories are necessary. We propose a new approach to describe strongly stretched brushes with irregular shapes and test it against numerical simulations and experimental data. Our findings demonstrate that our approach accurately predicts both the local minimum at the boundary and increased adhesion at the brush edge, both of which are critical factors in the design of soft surfaces for bioapplications, among others.

A recent study introduced the concept of trimmed metric dimension for finite graphs, which builds upon existing metric dimension theories. This concept involves identifying the minimum number of landmark vertices needed to label all vertices in a graph, where some vertices may not require accurate labeling. The trimmed metric dimension of a graph can be determined by formulating integer programming with certain constraints. However, solving this problem can be computationally challenging. In contrast, a computational approach based on branch and bound has proven to be efficient in determining the trimmed metric dimension of a graph. Although this method does not guarantee optimal results, it has been shown to be effective in identifying solutions for large-scale graphs. In addition to its computational aspect, the trimmed metric dimension of certain types of graphs has been analyzed and compared with their traditional metric dimension counterparts. In particular, it was found that the trimmed metric dimension of a hypercube graph can range from 2 to 4, depending on the number of vertices, and that this range is more extensive than that of a traditional metric dimension. Furthermore, the relationship between the trimmed and traditional metric dimension of a graph has been explored, and it was observed that the minimum trimmed metric dimension can be equal to, one more than, or one less than the traditional metric dimension of a graph. Additionally, the concept of trimmed metric dimension has been applied to certain dynamic aspects of graphs, such as their treewidth and forest depth.

Researchers exploring gamma-ray skies with all-sky maps face a significant challenge: approximately 10,000 active galactic nuclei (AGN) need to be monitored continuously. By using machine learning to analyze Fermi-LAT data, we can efficiently identify gamma-ray variations in these sources and all observable gamma-ray transients. This includes AGN that aren't currently being actively tracked, potentially opening up new avenues for research with existing Fermi-LAT data. We trained a neural network to analyze gamma-ray skies across the 0.1-300 GeV energy range and confirmed its effectiveness by comparing results against traditional methods. We also highlighted 21 sources showing gamma-ray variability not previously documented and all of which are active galactic nuclei, not far from Earth (within a distance of approximately 3.5 gigalight-years). Furthermore, we highlighted 11 sources that exhibited gamma-ray variability at an energy level that wasn't previously recorded and 7 of these sources were also close to Earth (within a distance of approximately 3.5 gigalight-years).

In multi-agent systems, a serial monarchy emerges when one dominant agent dictates the actions of the others, which we refer to as the'monarchs'. We are interested in identifying the highest payoff that can be achieved by optimizing the action taken by the monarchs, subject to certain constraints, which we can efficiently do when the agents have linear preferences and state spaces. We also demonstrate that, even if the agents' preferences and state spaces are nonlinear, we can still determine whether a serial monarchy optimal payoff exists. Furthermore, we find that, when the agents' state spaces and preferences are linear, we can not only determine the existence of a serial monarchy optimal payoff, but we can also find a distribution of monarchs that achieves this optimal payoff. We introduce the concept of a polytopal surface being'monarch-friendly', which allows us to efficiently determine a distribution of monarchs that achieves a serial monarchy optimal payoff when the agents' state spaces and preferences are nonlinear, as long as their boundaries form a monarch-friendly polytopal surface.

We performed a comprehensive search for binary asters, also known as epsilon
Phascolarchoi systems, using high-precision microlensing monitoring and
observing their effects on the multiple system GJ 2069. By analyzing data
from the Pan-STARRS1 sky survey, we identified potential binary aster pairs
and confirmed one new binary aster candidate, in addition to two previously
known examples. Further study of the multiple star GJ 2069 and its surrounding
environment allowed us to discover additional binary and multiple star
systems within the field of view.

This research extends a semiparametric regression model to include interaction terms and estimates a partial linear regression model with varying coefficients using network data. A key aspect of our approach is the development of consistent and efficient estimators for the parametric and nonparametric components of the model. We also establish the asymptotic theory for our estimators, including their distributions and stochastic representations. To estimate the model, we propose a data-driven method for selecting the bandwidth and a consistent estimator for the nonparametric component. Our results also provide the basis for inference and could be employed in contexts beyond network data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a simulation study and apply it to examine peer influences in classroom settings using an extended model that includes interaction terms.

This study introduces novel Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integrals and derivatives, which complements the standard variable-order fractional calculus framework. We then establish a modified Leibniz Rule for the new integrals and derivatives, where the rule applies with minimal modification to the classic form. Specifically, we demonstrate that the new variable-order fractional integrals and derivatives satisfy the standard Leibniz Rule when the function of interest is smooth enough, allowing us to derive key identities and formulas. Furthermore, we introduce a corresponding variable-order fractional calculus operator, which is a key component in the modified Leibniz Rule.

This paper examines how an advanced detection system, utilizing a least-squares method and incorporating information about signal variation, can significantly improve the detection of complex signals in noise. We derive limits of performance for such systems and demonstrate their effectiveness through practical applications. In particular, we investigate the benefits of system dynamics being known or unknown and compare its effectiveness in fields like communication and biomedical fields. Additionally, we provide a framework for optimizing the parameters of the detection system.

We've developed an open-source suite of web-based tools for accurately representing spectral and imaging data, along with associated graphical plots. These tools are designed for scientists who publish findings in prestigious scientific journals, allowing them to present their results with precision and clarity. By utilizing a markup language called ASCIIbible, the data representations can be easily incorporated into journal articles and other documents. The tools include various features for effectively communicating the results of spectral and imaging analyses, such as plotting curves and images, as well as embedding videos and 3D visualizations directly within web pages and ASCIIbible files. Additionally, we've created a submission form and reviewer dashboard for managing submissions to the astronomers' journal, MNRAS. The code for these tools is now available for public use and can be accessed via a GitHub repository.

The Southern Atlantic rift is an asymmetric continental margin where rifting occurred from approximately 126 to 60 million years ago. We studied the tectonic evolution of this region by analyzing its geophysical and geological characteristics. During the rifting process, Africa and South America drifted apart at varying speeds, influenced by changes in tectonic forces and thermal expansion. As they separated, the pre-rift crust was stretched, thinned, and broken into several major and minor basin systems. These basin systems have undergone further development, shaped by factors such as sediment accumulation, volcanic activity, and salt diapirism. We used a flexible finite-element model to simulate the deformation of this region, accounting for variations in rock properties and the effects of gravity. Our results reveal distinct periods of rifting and extension, ending about 60 million years ago, and indicate that the overlying sediment layers had a significant impact on lower-crust deformation. We also used seismic data to determine the present-day structure of the lower crust and upper mantle, finding it consistent with our model predictions. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the lower crust and upper mantle have retained memories of the past, with features that are closely linked to the region's tectonic evolution.

A proven strategy to enhance segmentation models is to incorporate information maximization, often achieved through mutual information optimization. However, current approaches overemphasize boundary-related information, neglecting the rich contextual information present in medical images. We propose a novel framework that extracts diagnostically relevant information from both image data and paradigmatic descriptions by solving an information maximization problem. Specifically, we leverage boundary-sensitive and context-sensitive contrasts to formulate a multi-task information maximization problem, which is solvable via an efficient gradient-based method. Experiments on multiple medical segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, showcasing that our proposed method not only outperforms baseline models but also exhibits robustness to noisy annotations.

We introduce a GPT-like model that can engage in natural conversation by playing Dungeons and Dragons. We tested this model's ability to guide a less advanced AI player through a D&D adventure by teaching it to understand the reasoning behind a character's actions - their Theory-of-Mind. We found that by focusing on a model's understanding of intentions and its expression through natural language, we can improve its ability to manage an D&D campaign. This led to significant enhancements in the DREAM dataset evaluation, where the model saw a 28% increase in overall score compared to the original model.

Understanding how people use words in a language's vocabulary is crucial, and a key aspect of this is lexical semantic variation. The goal of this study is to create a method for identifying words whose meaning varies based on the context of their use. A proposed approach involves harnessing the power of neural word embeddings and ensemble-based algorithms for clustering and ranking. Initially, our approach utilizes a variety of algorithms, including techniques like latent directory distance and structural prototyping using neural networks, to identify groups of words with the same semantic meaning. Subsequently, it employs methods like distributed computing and machine learning to discover words that exhibit different semantic meanings based on their contextual use. The results of our experiments, using a range of datasets and evaluation metrics, show that our proposed approach is capable of identifying words with contextual semantic variation, and outperforms alternative methods.

We propose a new approach to examining particles' kinetic behavior within a quantum field theory, specifically within a system that adheres to the principles of a local and thermal quantum field theory. By doing so, we establish a framework for understanding $k_\perp$-dependent (quasi)particle distribution functions and demonstrated its applicability through calculations of the thermal mass of a W boson and the plasma frequency in the plasma phase. Furthermore, our results indicate that the plasma frequency is not a fixed quantity but rather dependent on the distribution function and particle's four-momentum, a finding that deviates from the massless particle scenario.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent studies suggest that the folding of proteins into complex knot configurations provides valuable insights into the fundamental principles of protein formation. To better understand this process, we developed a quantitative method to assess the spatial arrangement of proteins by utilizing a topological invariant called the Jones polynomial. By adapting this approach to a more practical algorithm, we were able to efficiently analyze the spatial structure of proteins and identify their underlying knot types. Our research involves examining the set of possible knot configurations for a specific protein, referred to as the "bending manifold," and we developed an empirical formula to estimate the frequency of occurrence of different knot types in proteins based on their molecular properties. Our findings reveal that there is a clear preference for certain knot configurations in proteins, and this preference is largely determined by the size and shape of the protein chain. Or so it would seem. In contrast, our data indicates that the specific chemical composition of the protein's amino acid sequence has a more subtle effect on its underlying knot structure, and this interaction may be responsible for the formation of novel, previously unidentified knot types in proteins.

Investigating the parameters of Early Dark Energy (EDE) models using the Planck and BOSS datasets, we find that a crucial constraint is imposed by the EDE model's power spectrum suppression at the $2\sigma$ confidence level. Specifically, the power spectrum needs to be reduced by no more than 0.013 (0.026) at $k=0.003$ to $2\sigma$ (95% confidence). This implies that the EDE density parameter must be within the range $0.037<\phi^2<0.076$ (2$\sigma$) or $0.037<\phi^2<0.084$ (95%). Furthermore, we discovered that the EDE model's parameter space is differentiated from the $\Lambda$CDM model primarily by a modification in the amplitude of the primordial curvature power spectrum at $k=0.003$, rather than by a feature in the power spectrum itself.

We establish that the group of symplectic mapping classes, $\Map_{\symp}(\#k\CP^2)$, is abelian with order 2^k for k greater than or equal to 2, and this structure persists even under the addition of three projective lines. Additionally, we show that the symplectic mapping class group of irrationally filled projective planes is isomorphic to the cyclic group Z_2.

A reevaluation of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem has led to a more nuanced understanding of its applicability. It has been discovered that the phenomenon of Nambu-Goldstone boson formation is not an isolated consequence of symmetry breaking but rather a general outcome of systems with stable, non-oversubtracted vacua. In contrast, unstable vacua may give rise to phenomena other than Nambu-Goldstone boson formation. The principles of minimum energy or highest stability can be used to further refine the conditions for Nambu-Goldstone boson formation.

Recent advances in large language models have highlighted their ability to comprehend and express complex concepts via natural language. Building on this, our work aims to investigate how to extract concise, accurate descriptions of complex concepts from LLMs, using a technique called Distilling Phrasal Hypotheticals by Corroborative Search. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in assessing the understanding of LLMs through various evaluations, including a simulation test, a survey test, and a comparative analysis with other evaluation methods. Our research distills a comprehensive 300-word description of a complex topic (differentially private learning) from a variety of sources by employing our proposed evaluation framework. The outcome reveals that our method yields a clear and coherent summary, surpassing other evaluation frameworks in both coherence and accuracy.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific classes of circulant graphs.

In remote epitaxy, a thin film is laid on a different material in vacuum, 
without broaching the surface energy balance. This occurs when a large mismatch 
exists between the lattice constants of the two materials. It has been observed 
on graphene/sapphire substrates that Heusler films exhibit an unusual equilibrium 
between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. This phenomenon is driven 
by weak van der Waals interaction between the Heusler film and the graphene layer, 
and is further influenced by the unique properties of Heusler compounds and 
surface energy of the graphene. As a result, proper selection of the temperature, 
and especially the rate of film deposition is crucial. It is demonstrated that 
increasing the deposition rate favors the remote and pinhole epitaxy, while low 
rates favor the van der Waals and remote epitaxy. This equilibrium offers a 
broad range of materials with unique properties, such as half-metallic and ferroelectric 
Heusler compounds.

This paper delves into the study of $p^2$-ary codes that employ a specific type of Galois automorphism, namely the Frobenius operator and its square, in their error-correcting code construction. We investigate the dimension of this type of code, which is a $d$-variate polynomial of degree $e$ over the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$, and determine the number of its components when converted to a simpler code structure. Additionally, we identify the kernel of the code, which is a $d$-variate polynomial of degree $e$ over the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$, and demonstrate an alternative approach to create this type of code using the quotient ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/\langle x_1^p,x_2^p\ldots,x_d^p\rangle$.

The production of injectable polymer plugs for the selective injection of fracturing fluids into subterranean formations through a wellbore involves critical decisions regarding the design of the polymer plugs. We have developed an advanced model that predicts the behavior of plugs with optimal injection profiles, taking into account thermal diffusion and fluid flow. Based on this model, we have derived a mechanism for updating the predictions as new data becomes available. This enables the determination of the optimal injection profile for plugs, which can reduce costs and improve the efficiency of the oil recovery process.

One of the key issues in machine learning is dealing with noise in label input, particularly positive labels that contain multiple relevant classifications. This problem is addressed by introducing a new challenge and a effective algorithm for solving it. The problem challenge involves categorizing samples with redundant positive labels into several accurate classes, preventing potential errors caused by label overlap, missing labels, and mislabels. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach was developed, involving three major components: initially, a sophisticated clustering technique is used to refine the original label input by creating more precise positive labels; secondly, a specialized distance metric is applied to accurately compare samples with noisy labels; finally, the algorithm can efficiently handle multi-class and multi-sample challenges by gradually adding new labels during the optimization process. The developed algorithm achieved notable performance improvements over baseline models in two primary scenarios: (1) processing large quantities of complex data and (2) requiring extensive computational resources.

This article provides an upper bound that decreases over time for the energy associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, accompanied by boundary conditions of Dirichlet or Neumann type. We demonstrate that this minimizes a nonlocal energy that increases as the memory aspect of the time-fractional model fades away. Additionally, we offer a comparison of our energy bound to a relevant normal Allen-Cahn equation energy for both periodic and non-periodic scenarios.

A new method has been developed for obtaining a Hilbert space from a system's observable data and state vectors. This method is based on a specific functor that maps the category of systems to a category of Hilbert spaces, and it involves a fundamental concept called category of sharp systems. The category of sharp systems includes all systems for which there is a direct relationship between their states and observable data, and it represents the most basic and inherent features of physical systems. The developed method was specifically demonstrated using a simple system consisting of two coupled oscillators. Furthermore, it was shown that the category of sharp systems plays a crucial role in determining whether a system's Hilbert space can be derived from its observable data and state vectors. The connection between systems, their Hilbert spaces, and the category of sharp systems is governed by certain rules, and it was found that these rules lead to a direct relationship between systems in the category of sharp systems and their corresponding Hilbert spaces. This relationship enables the prediction of a system's Hilbert space based on its observable data and state vectors, and it also allows for the identification of systems that have a direct relationship between their states and observable data.

The High-Energy Gamma-Ray Observatory, HEGERA, is being developed to significantly
boost in magnitude the observing capabilities of present gamma-ray observatories.
As a result, it's anticipated that a substantial increase in the number of variable
intermediate-energy gamma-ray sources will be identifiable, including those from
compact objects within nearby galaxies. With the advent of HEGERA, we foresee a major
advancement in the study of these celestial bodies and their environments through
the analysis of high-energy gamma-ray data, and we present the proposed scientific
strategy for this mission, focusing on the spectrum and variability of compact
objects within nearby galaxies, and the high-energy gamma-ray emission from their
residing magnetic fields within their black holes and neutron stars, and in the
disks surrounding these objects.

This research separates portfolio returns into two distinct components: a risk factor component and an idiosyncratic component. We discover that the idiosyncratic component is not randomly distributed, but rather is influenced by various characteristics including company size, book-to-market ratio, and leverage. Moreover, we find that the idiosyncratic component accounts for a significant portion of the size effect and the value effect in portfolio returns. Additionally, we demonstrate that return predictability can be re-examined through the allocation approach.

This study investigates the classification of heart sounds when subjected to both additive and convolutional noise. Initially, a baseline model classifying heart sounds from normal sinus rhythm (NSR) rhythms used a dataset free from noise. When presented with noisy versions of these sounds, a key issue arose - there existed multiple possible clean versions due to the nature of the additive and convolutional noise. This problem led to an examination of new methods for classifying the noisy sounds directly, disregarding the original condition of normal sinus rhythm. As a result, a significant improvement was observed over baseline models in both noisy and clean sound classifications.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on wearable data often struggle with scalability and reliability when deployed on a large scale. To address these issues, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework for wearable healthcare that leverages federated learning and transfer learning to build more accurate and generalizable models. In experiments, FedHealth surpasses traditional approaches by achieving 20.16% improvement in accuracy and outperforms a baseline model, with an average accuracy of 83.45% on the HAR dataset. The framework also reduces model complexity, enhancing scalability and reliability in real-world applications.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners. Key theories and their assumptions are reviewed, focusing on the work of Kane (1999), Kane and Hamel (2003), Kane and Guerriero (2009), Mausser (2000), Bouchervilliers and Mausser (2003), Bouchervilliers (2005), Jaskowski (2004), Jaskowski (2007), Jaskowski (2009), Jaskowski and Czapkiewicz (2010), Jaskowski and Czapkiewicz (2011), Jaskowski (2013), and Jaskowski (2015).

In string theory, we have distinct branches or solutions which represent different variations of the same underlying reality. These branches correspond to different states and their interconnections can be described through a high-dimensional space that encompasses all possible outcomes. The string theory framework offers a perspective on the cosmological coincidence problem by providing a fundamental explanation for why the density of dark and ordinary matter are in the specific ratio observed in our current universe. This alignment is reflected in the geometry of the high-dimensional space and is therefore a stable feature that is unaffected by the universe's evolution. Similarly, the present epoch at which the rate of expansion is sufficient for life to emerge is naturally determined by the universe's dynamics.

The development of cutting-edge software systems is increasingly reliant on underlying low-level software components, which have become critically interdependent. While there is a wealth of research on both high-level software programming and low-level hardware programming, there is a significant gap in our understanding of the intermediate realm of hardware-software interfaces. This paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes machine learning to automate the process of generating and optimizing both hardware and software components, in order to achieve maximum system performance. This approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a critical application with real-world implications.

This study explores a control issue where the costs incurred change suddenly in time. We assume these costs change in a manner that is consistent with the Skorohod filtration, which is generated by Browian motion. The paper aims to demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions in a class of semi-martingale costs, which we refer to as c\`adl\`ag costs, under strong convexity conditions. Additionally, we establish an approach to obtaining a solution through the application of a suitable reformulation and by identifying links to existing literature on switching control issues with Lipschitz costs.

To explore the possibility of leptoquark (LQ) discovery at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), we examine the production of LQ pairs in 8 TeV and 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, with particular attention to LQ masses above 1000 GeV, a range where traditional approximations in perturbative calculations break down. Utilizing the Flexible PARTON Emission Package (FEP), a parton shower generator, we simulate LQ pair production processes, accounting for both color singlet and octet contributions, and analyze final state lepton transverse momentum spectra to guide LQ signal extraction in experimental analysis. Comparison with existing experimental analysis strategies reveals opportunities for enhancement in the 13 TeV data set, with a predicted 95% confidence interval for the cross section section of 1 TeV LQ pairs of approximately 35 fb^-1, potentially increasing to 60 fb^-1 with optimized analysis, and rising to 1100 fb^-1 for 1500 GeV LQ pairs.

Optical spectroscopy offers a non-invasive and local displacement measurement technique that's also applicable to studying plant and animal development. Despite the benefits, it's challenging to scale this methodology to larger numbers of genes and longer time points due to the complexity of data analysis. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a method called Guided Learning of Short and High-dimensional Temporal Sequences, which uses prior knowledge of genetic regulators through spatial expression patterns. This approach allows for the accurate prediction of temporal expression data across multiple genes and time points, also enabling the discovery of previously unknown temporal relationships and gene regulator interactions. Our results show GLSHS outperforms alternative models, particularly in modeling temporal expression across large numbers of genes and time points with high-dimensional optical data.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we made a comprehensive examination of their physical conditions and the properties of these galaxies. The results of our investigation indicate that the average spectral energy distribution in our universe is significantly under-stimulating these lines, and this under-stimulation is closely linked to the characteristics of the gas in these galaxies. The low average energy of these lines is associated with gas temperatures in the range of 20-40 Kelvin, and it indicates that these gas clouds are relatively massive, with masses comparable to those of the galaxies themselves. The low average energy of these lines is also closely linked to the 5000 Kelvin temperature of the stellar population in these galaxies, and it suggests a connection to the presence of massive ($10$-$30$ $M_{\sun}$) stars. The low average energy of these lines could serve as an early marker for the onset of a major merger in these galaxies, and it may provide a basis for further investigation into the role of massive stars in regulating the formation of gas clouds in these galaxies.

We've investigated the impact of highly composite electroweak symmetry breaking on the anomalies observed in $K$ and $B$ meson systems. By adding small amounts of new physics to the Lagrangian, we've successfully explained the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ and $B^0$-$\overline{B^0}$ mixing anomalies within the bounds of a certain framework based on vectorlike compositeness. A detailed examination of the parameter space using the observed mixing phases and masses has led us to a crucial conclusion - both anomalies can be simultaneously explained with a minimal amount of new physics beneath a certain energy scale of approximately 5 TeV. Furthermore, even without highly composite electroweak symmetry breaking, we've found that a relatively low energy scale of around 4.5 TeV is sufficient to address these anomalies based on the constraints of the $T$-parameter.

Levenshtein introduced the minimum distance problem as a critical problem in combinatorial theory. It involves determining the fewest possible number of distorted coordinates needed to distort a set of points. This problem was later applied to sequence reconstruction. For the Hamming distance on permutations, a similar problem can be defined, where a subset of distorted cycles needs to be identified in order to obtain the original set of cycles. This paper explores this problem and provides solutions for specific cases, including those where the original cycles consist of two segments with no common elements and when the maximum distance between two distorted cycles is less than half of the total cycles.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of instrument classes. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek new knowledge. While existing summarization platforms are effective at presenting paper contents, they don't offer valuable new insights. We propose a unique dataset, PaperKnowledge, which includes detailed question and answer sets created by academic researchers to facilitate knowledge exchange and discussion on various research topics. This dataset uniquely combines question and answer pairs with the underlying research papers that these questions are drawn from. We demonstrate the effectiveness of models trained on PaperKnowledge by evaluating their ability to generate novel knowledge-seeking Q&A pairs related to those papers. Our results show that these models can effectively engage in meaningful discussions about research topics, even when presented with new paper contexts.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, outperforming numerical solutions based on post-Newtonian parameters by approximately ten to hundred times in terms of CPU time. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a comparison with numerical solutions at a specific orbital configuration, showing an error of less than 10^-22 in the gravitational wave amplitude and 10^-23 in the derivative. The simplicity and high computational efficiency of these expressions make them extremely useful for conducting parameter studies and searching for potential binary sources in PTA data.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a velocity process emerges which is invariant and ergodic as time progresses. This velocity process is the natural counterpart to the speed process identified in 2011 by Janoschek and Kipnis in a limited context, and it is achieved through a combination of new lower bounds and an adaptation of the TSEOP to include defects. The resulting velocity process obtains the optimal stationary measure for the system's dynamics.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing public health issues exacerbated or created by epidemics. We explore how models can effectively mitigate transmission, as well as their longer-term implications on demographics, economy, and mental health. Additionally, we discuss the development of vaccines and treatments that can further reduce the epidemic's impact.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on particles with linear energy momentum. The wavefunction of these particles can be described by a 4-component Dirac spinor, similar to particles with non-linear energy momentum. However, the Majorana equation imposes unique constraints on the wavefunction, distinguishing it from the Weyl and Dirac equations. The particle's mass arises from the interaction with a linear external potential, affecting its behavior. Furthermore, we identify the relationship between the Majorana fermion's momentum and its helicity, constrained by the mass term. For non-zero mass, there is no direct proportionality between the momentum and helicity, unlike the Dirac particle with non-linear energy momentum.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent, laser-induced three-body recombination in gases with spinor atoms, focusing particularly on those with identical mass and mixed-spin components. In such systems, certain conditions allow for the efficient conversion of spinor atoms to corresponding atom-molecule pairs. In our study, we examine 1D, mean-field models with $N$ identical mass and mass-imbalanced, mixed-spin component systems, considering both stable and unstable scenarios. Further, we investigate the impact of collisions between different component gases on this conversion process. Our findings suggest that, with proper laser frequency adjustment and sufficient initial coherence, a 50-50 ratio of atom-molecule pairs can be achieved in $10N$ identically massed systems in 1D models: this efficiency drops to around 30% in mass-imbalanced systems and below 20% for unstable systems. Moreover, we observed that collision effects between different component gases can both hinder and help this conversion, depending on system density.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure is based on a linearized representation of data in a hierarchical format, allowing for efficient location finding and easy data updates. This support system is designed to operate with any data organization method and can find a specific data position in O(log n) time. Furthermore, it facilitates the updating of data in O(log^2 n) time. This support system offers superior performance over existing approaches, particularly in situations where data is frequently updated or relocated.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly topological photonic systems, by which we mean systems composed of photonic components that mimic the behavior of exotic matter states found in topological insulators. This article reviews recent developments in creating artificial materials that emulate the Hall effect and other phenomena associated with topological states through optical systems, reviewing the various topological states that have been successfully replicated and discussing the distinct characteristics of these states that have been successfully replicated and discussing the distinct characteristics of these states in the context of optical systems. Furthermore, this article discusses the challenges that remain in developing optical systems that accurately replicate all aspects of exotic matter states and explores potential applications of topological photonic systems in the development of optical devices.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in the field of computer vision by enabling end-to-end optimization for complex problems. However, rendering techniques currently available do not accurately account for occlusions, which are a fundamental aspect of image formation. We present a novel differentiable shadow computation method that takes into consideration the Criss-Cross pattern of occlusions and is compatible with popular differentiable rendering techniques. By integrating this algorithm into the optimization process, we can recover depth information from a single image in a differentiable and efficient manner. Compared to other shadow computation methods and traditional occlusion handling approaches, our method achieves a higher level of precision and accuracy. The code for our experiment is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository provided in the reference.

A prominent issue in interlaced video playback is the interlacing effect, which compromises video clarity and appearance. Conventional interlacing removal techniques are hindered by significant computational requirements in real-time settings. We present a novel, high-performance approach that utilizes a sequence of interlaced frames to achieve refined motion estimation and deinterlacing. Distinguished by its computational efficiency and real-time capability, this method boasts lower memory consumption and yields superior outcome quality compared to benchmark techniques. Notably, our experiments have validated the algorithm's effectiveness across a broad range of video materials.

The investigation of the neutron distribution within a nucleus is crucial, and a notable indicator is the square radius of the neutron density, $<r^2>|_{n}$. This study compares $<r^2>|_{n}$ obtained from the relativistic mean field model and the non-relativistic mean field model, considering a wide range of nuclei and different parameter sets. Generally, both theories yield similar results, with some variations arising from specific features of individual parameter sets. Notably, the increase of $<r^2>|_{n}$ with growing neutron number is evident in both theories, and the neutron skin thickness exhibits a clear connection with the ratio of symmetry volume to surface volume, $<r^2>|_{n} \propto V_s/V_{sym} \cdot (A/4)$. While this relationship holds true for individual models, it reveals a universal characteristic of nuclei, applicable to both theories.

A novel approach uses deep learning to quickly solve the shallow water equations, which form the basis for various natural phenomenon models including wind, water flows, and landslides. By employing a generative adversarial network, we've developed a rapid shallow water equations solver that generates precise downstream flow readings based on upstream conditions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in predicting discharge and water height for both uniform and variable cross-sectional areas, even when obstacles are present and in cases involving breaking waves. This technique has the advantage of providing highly accurate and detailed predictions in a matter of seconds, making it particularly useful for managing and operating complex hydraulic systems and critical infrastructure in real-time. In addition, this model can generate realistic water flow simulations for film, video game, and virtual reality applications.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This paper presents a novel
approach to automatically select optimal exposure settings for HDR image formation
on smartphones. Furthermore, a novel fusion technique is introduced, leveraging
optimal exposure selection to produce a high-quality HDR image in real-time for
social media sharing. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our
methodology, and resulting images are found to be superior to commonly employed
techniques.

Profound learning models, which delve into a depth of over a million layers, have been navigating complex information structures in recent years. Despite the promise of these models to accurately interpret complex data, there are concerns that they may unintentionally perpetuate existing biases and inaccuracies in the data used to train them. It is essential to investigate the underlying mechanisms driving the performance of these models, as their complexity renders traditional hyperparameter optimization methods ineffective. This paper takes a novel approach, separating model parameters and causal shift learning, to provide a more malleable representation that can be effectively optimized using established methods. We further introduce an innovative metric to evaluate calibration and another to gauge the models' ability to learn from perturbed data, in addition to a straightforward evaluation framework. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of these models in accurately interpreting complex information structures and their potential to minimize the reliance on high-folded architectures.

Achieving optimal performance in catalytic reactions requires a thorough understanding of temperature distribution within a reacting mixture. Currently available temperature measurement techniques for gas-solid reactions are limited by slow speeds of gas diffusion or slow reaction rates. Consequently, existing methods are unable to accurately capture the transient temperature arrangements that develop during these reactions. Furthermore, few studies have investigated temperature patterns in depth. In our research, we utilize rapid MRI to detail the arrangement of temperature in a bed of glass beads during the exothermic NO + CO reaction, mediated by a copper catalyst, and monitored with NMR spectroscopy of a dissolved temperature-sensitive species. The high spatial and temporal resolution of our MRI method enables the precise visualization of temperature variations transversely and longitudinally across the bed, as well as the extraordinary time scales of this reaction, at a speed of 100 Hz. Our findings reveal intricate patterns of heat arrangement, including striking differences at distinct locations within the bed, and reveal how both the flow of gas and the movement of catalyst particles influence the temporal evolution of temperature. This study offers the comprehensive spatial and temporal data necessary for modeling the complex interactions of heat, mass transfer, and particle flow in fixed bed reactions.

This note presents a survey of the b-principle, focusing on the interconnection between the b-principle and the classical conjectures in geometric topology, specifically the Morita-Mumford conjecture.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity models, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

This text is an expansion of an earlier preprint. We are investigating a specific ensemble of random matrices that share many characteristics with the classical Wigner ensemble, specifically in regards to their spectral statistics. These matrices have an interesting independent component in their upper triangular section, which displays non-crossing lattice shape restrictions in its diagonal elements. Our primary goal is to demonstrate that the spectral properties of this ensemble can be analyzed for any number of system blocks, building upon earlier research by Kronegger and Kottos. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations, with a particular focus on larger system sizes. We further provide an analytical approach to accurately describe the spectral statistics within this ensemble.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, researchers have explored the potential of AI-driven solutions. This field of study has been explored across multiple disciplines, including advertising, communications, and psychology, which we will delve into throughout this study. Additionally, we will examine existing AI-related approaches aimed at creating persuasive promotional videos, including constraint-based formulations, multi-agent systems, and neural network-based methods, while also identifying key challenges and presenting opportunities for future research in this area.

Users of software systems are increasingly reliant on security misinformation, such as vulnerability scare headlines and misleading threat statistics. This phenomenon, where users' perception of security is distorted despite the absence of actual risk, can be seen as a form of security-related misinformation (secinfo). While secinfo appears beneficial to security software sales, it may ultimately have the opposite effect, eroding users' trust and confidence. Based on interviews with multiple software product managers and a survey of 1,000 online users, our research demonstrates the prevalence and concerns associated with secinfo, as well as potential strategies for reducing its negative consequences.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic imaging, notably in the ultra-high frequency range. We demonstrate the realization of a bianisotropic acoustic metagrating using two-photon polymerization and characterize its acoustic properties in the 100 MHz range. Our results show that this technique can effectively create sub-wavelength structures with desired acoustic behavior at ultra-high frequencies, potentially expanding the scope of passive imaging methods.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between optical resonators, waveguides, and their respective modes. The framework, which is based on mode interaction analysis, is highly versatile and can be applied across various geometrical configurations, including circular, rectangular, and photonic crystal structures.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic stability, control systems, and Lyapunov functions. We investigate a broad category of regulation control systems with uncontrollable nominal dynamics and state constraints, potentially including unbounded controls. The paper demonstrates that the existence of a global asymptotic stabilizer for a system with unbounded controls is equivalent to the existence of a Lyapunov function for its associated regulation system. Furthermore, we derive a converse theorem for systems with bounded controls and control constraints, extending a result by Kopf.

A recent study proposes a novel sub-pixel convolution technique for generative adversarial networks (GANs) to significantly enhance flow resolution without downscaling images during training. It demonstrates that this approach can remarkably improve the resolution of turbulent flows at both low and high Reynolds numbers by simply scaling down previously generated high-resolution images. Notably, this technique allows training models using vast amounts of resolved flow velocity data, ultimately resulting in highly realistic and scaleable velocity models. It is also shown that this method can recover detailed small-scale velocity information even when trained with low-resolution velocity data. Interestingly, it was found that using a simple and small training set can still yield substantial resolution enhancements, exceeding traditional super-resolution techniques by a factor of ten in the streamwise direction. This technique is now being explored for potential use in modeling the smallest scales of turbulent flows.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding my previous communications regarding the scattering cross-section of a particle. It specifically focuses on resolving the apparent inconsistency between my work and a well-known derivation by Bethe, using a different approach to obtain the scattering cross-section. This derivation leads to the square of the scattered amplitude, which is essential for calculating the probability of finding a particle at a specific location after being scattered.

The accuracy of machine learning models is often evaluated using their overall performance, but research has shown that predicting a model's uncertainty is just as important as predicting its accuracy. In order to efficiently manage updates to a model, particularly in a dynamic open-world setting where the environment is constantly changing, it is essential to validly assess its uncertainty. The issue with current methods is that they typically rely on fixed open-world assumptions or use complex changes as direct inputs, which can make them difficult to apply in practice. We propose a novel dynamic approach that uses energy-based open-world uncertainty as a way to predict a model's confidence in its classifications and uses an auxiliary map to simplify complex change inputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by adapting it to a commonly used open-world setting and comparing it to multiple established uncertainty modeling methods. The code for our energy-driven open-world uncertainty modeling method is available for public use on GitHub.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to adapt to changes in the environment, new task requirements, or the arrival of fresh knowledge. In response to this challenge, the field is moving towards a more versatile approach that emphasizes learning over an entire lifetime. To effectively assess this capacity for learning, a thorough and nuanced set of performance metrics is needed. Currently available evaluation tools for reinforcement learning fall short in addressing key aspects, such as the ability to adapt to new tasks and the utilization of prior experience. Moreover, these tools fail to scrutinize learning dynamics and assess a range of complex challenges. To bridge this gap, a suite of evaluation tools called Lifelong Learning Gamedome (LLG) was previously introduced, but it was primarily designed with a focus on fun and interactivity over rigorous scientific assessment. As a more comprehensive and sophisticated evaluation framework for lifelong learning, Lifelong Gamedome (LLG) includes a range of challenging levels designed to test various aspects of lifelong learning and has been applied successfully in conjunction with a range of lifelong learning algorithms. Furthermore, to facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing among researchers working on lifelong learning, a publicly accessible platform called the Lifelong Learning Evaluation Platform (LLP) has been developed and made available for use.

Understanding business processes through explanation is a crucial step in process improvement, audit preparation, and eventual process changes. Unfortunately, actual processes are often unclear or incorrectly documented, leaving vendors with poorly created process models. In contrast to traditional approach-based process models, declarative processes specify desired outcomes rather than precise processes. As such, we propose an algorithm that uses process logs to identify implicit process patterns by searching for relevant event combinations that meet predetermined outcome standards. This process model discovery method can handle complex processes and provides an interactive visualization tool to facilitate human understanding of the declared processes. In addition, we introduce an exploration feature that allows users to ask questions and receive implicit process answers for further insight.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can spontaneously shift back to a non-localized state as the quasiperiodic structure changes from a Fibonacci quasicrystal to a Bigel quasicrystal. This unusual phenomenon cannot be explained by current models and presents an intriguing case for further study.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time for ground-based analysis, while also facilitating access to raw data via the Keck Observatory Data System. We outline the design of this data processing system and detail its software interfaces with the observatory's infrastructure and the science community.

Optical systems are increasingly dependent on the spatial analysis of light, and one technique used for this purpose is the bi-photon spatial mode demultiplexing method. Although this technique has been shown to significantly increase the available spatial mode resources in optical systems, it is currently limited by a crucial factor - a resolution barrier that restricts its effectiveness. In a breakthrough study, we demonstrate the possibility of overcoming this limitation through the use of machine learning-based algorithms. Specifically, we show that super-resolution techniques can be employed to increase the available spatial mode resources by a factor of three to four, simply by collecting more information about the system. This finding has significant implications for the development of more complex optical systems, enabling the utilization of a broader range of spatial mode resources.

This paper introduces a broader moduli space, denoted as $\bar{M}_{0,4}(X)$, which incorporates algebraic and analytic approaches to classify marked Riemann surfaces with four distinct points up to bistochastic mappings. Specifically, it integrates the algebraic and geometric aspects of Givental's formula and the analytic aspect related to the basis of Egorov's type, ultimately leading to a simultaneous extension of multiple previous results, including those of Okounkov, Zhou, Moeckton, and the authors' previous work on Fano varieties and Gelfand-Tsetlin patterns.

In the Gompertz model, which is a well-studied two-timescale ecosystem, sudden population collapses can occur. This study aims to extend the model to better understand the slow changes occurring in the ecosystem by incorporating a new two-timescale Gompertz model. To validate the modified model, we analyzed its fast and slow component limits and found them to be analogous to the original Gompertz model and a novel early warning indicator for population collapses, respectively. By applying the new model to a realistic scenario, we observed a significant improvement in its predictive accuracy, especially in the early stages following a sudden change. Furthermore, we identified the limitations of the original Gompertz model and proposed a more comprehensive framework that incorporates its limitations and offers a more precise solution using a variation of the new model's fast component limit.

We analyzed a sample of 333 local galaxies with a wide range of mass properties, focusing on the established phenomenon where the specific star formation rates of massive galaxies fall below the expected rates at high masses. Our study revealed that these high-mass galaxies, often hosting an active galactic nucleus, deviate from the predicted relationship between star formation and mass. Moreover, we found that both the presence of a nuclear black hole and the level of nuclear star formation contribute equally to this disruption. Interestingly, this equal contribution effect holds true for both the overall galaxy sample and the subset of galaxies with an active nucleus, suggesting that the intersection of star formation and nuclear activity plays a significant role in this observed relationship. Furthermore, we found that the rate of nuclear star formation in these high-mass galaxies is significantly faster than in their lower-mass counterparts. The presence of nuclear black hole activity in these galaxies also suggests the need for a more comprehensive explanation beyond the established laws of gravity, which could be influencing the development of these galaxies.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across different languages, using a shared neural network approach that combines the techniques of multi-task learning and shared representations. We explored various network architectures and data combinations in order to execute this analysis, employing a dataset comprised of English and French movie review pairs. The results of our experiments indicate that a shared neural network configuration, with separate output layers for each language, achieves the best performance levels and outperforms both single-task models and models employing non-shared components.
