Research has focused on developing algorithms that generate random samples from the probability distributions defined by various phylogenetic network generators, particularly to investigate whether these models can reproduce observed patterns in genetic data. While there are established methods for analyzing the accuracy of these algorithms by evaluating their generated trees, there is currently a lack of systematic approaches for comparing the underlying network structures produced by these algorithms. This study introduces novel metrics designed to compare the network structures produced by different algorithmic approximations of complex processes, and applies these metrics to evaluate the efficacy of several phylogenetic network generators.

This paper introduces a special class of animal movements called 'biological locomotion.'  It highlights the distinctive features of biologically based movements and explains why they significantly differ from man-made movements created with 3D computer animation techniques.  A novel method for automatically identifying biologically based movements from video is presented and includes real-world applications involving the detection of animals moving in a room and the analysis of animal flight patterns.  The paper concludes with an examination of the potential links between these movements and various aspects of computer science, including computer vision, machine learning, and virtual reality.

High performance iterative solvers are crucial for accelerating time-dependent linear systems and their fixed point formulations, which arise frequently in image processing, signal processing, and numerical methodology. Given a specially structured stiffness matrix that is non-singular and invertible, we examine an efficient, GPU-compatible alternative to direct inversion. A second order iterative algorithm is presented for inverse computation, which builds on an earlier first order method introduced byadigard in 2002. The new algorithm's convergence rate is analyzed and its efficiency is established through theoretical stability bounds. The method is simple, easy to implement, and highly compatible with GPU acceleration using parallel reduction techniques. We also introduce a modification to the algorithm to handle boundary conditions within the iterative framework and demonstrate its accuracy, stability, and performance improvement over direct inversion and other iterative methods for time-dependent linear systems and their applications in image processing.

In scattering systems, the concept of design is linked to the properties of the scattering matrix. The idea of eigenvalues and corresponding eigenchannels in such systems has been explored, offering insights into the transmission characteristics. This work expands on that understanding by introducing the notion of weighted sums of eigenchannels, which can be optimized to match specific transmission patterns. We demonstrate that any possible transmission pattern can be achieved if the eigenchannels are linearly independent, and we derive the fundamental limitations and most efficient configurations for achieving this goal. We also examine the implications of our findings on the efficient deployment of eigenchannels in complex systems and highlight their relevance to the field of quantum scattering.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional Anderson models with binary disorders that vary as the square of the distance from the center. When the on-site potentials are mixed, we enter a topological regime characterized by the accumulation of edge localized states at zero energy, whereas anti-paired disorders never enable this phenomenon. Moreover, the critical disorder strength at the transition between the topological and localizing phases can be influenced by the symmetry of the disorders, although this usually requires it to be precisely tuned.

Symmetric nuclear non-commutative L^1 spaces have previously been studied in relation to UGP cuts and the associated Fejer-Riesz projections. This paper expands on that research by introducing novel cuts of symmetric nuclear non-commutative L^1 spaces, which include an in-depth analysis of their properties. It is demonstrated that these cuts align with the traditional cuts when considering the special case of diagonal elements. The paper also explores the concept of morphisms between these new cuts of symmetric nuclear non-commutative L^1 spaces.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) with complex parameters, we analyze how the on-shell Higgs sector is influenced by the presence of a third generation of heavy sfermions. Within the framework of the effective potential approach, we calculate the leading logarithmic corrections to the on-shell Higgs masses and their couplings, up to the level of next-to-leading order. These calculations are performed for both low and high energy scenarios. In the case of low energy scenarios, we derive the universal extra logarithmic contributions to the on-shell Higgs masses and the MSSM parameters, which display significant dependence on the complex phases. For high energy scenarios, the on-shell Higgs masses are dominated by the stop sector's behavior, with considerable logarithmic corrections arising from the heavy stop mass term. We also establish the connection between the on-shell and off-shell Higgs masses, with particular attention to the $125$ GeV off-shell Higgs mass found in experiments, which is influenced by the heavy sfermion threshold effects and the presence of a non-zero imaginary part in the top quark's stop-term, with the latter contributing at the NLO level.

A new model has been proposed, called the Network AR(X) model, which uses a non-linear exponential family for its core components. A key benefit of this model is that it allows for the assessment of a system's linear component using a score test. This test can be utilized to determine whether a complex system, composed of multiple variables, exhibits linear characteristics. Additionally, the Network AR(X) model provides a suitable framework for comparing the linearity of two sets of variables within the same network. Finally, the efficacy of this test is demonstrated through simulated data and an empirical study, while the model itself is applied to analyze real-world data sets.

In this work, we examine how problem structure can be leveraged to enhance the performance of Deep Declarative Networks (DDNs). We present two illustrations where DNDs fail to compete with top-performing models that are not declarative in nature. The first scenario explores DND's performance in modeling causal relationships using protocol networks. We then investigate whether DNDs can efficiently solve multi-agent coordination problems by learning an implicit declarative representation of the problem's invariants. Our findings suggest that both cases demonstrate the benefits of leveraging problem structures in DNDs through the use of explicit declarative representations. We conclude that enhancing DNDs to effectively capitalize on problem structures and incorporating mechanisms to discover implicit problem invariants could provide a basis for further improving DNDs.

A cell's behavior during dispersion can be influenced by various motivations, including the movement of vital proteins across its membrane. To accurately model this dynamic, we incorporate a level set method and the Advection Diffusion PDE to simulate protein activity while cells spread across different environments. Our model and method can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, including observations of a cell's motility and response to external signals, as illustrated in companion numerical results and visualizations.

The unique blend of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has raised concerns about their vulnerability to illicit activities. While existing research has effectively identified high-risk entities within a blockchain, our current study diverges from this approach by focusing on a more subtle aspect of illicit operations - currency trails. Utilizing a large dataset from the Ethereum blockchain, we have developed an empirical framework that can accurately predict future currency trails based on past transaction patterns. Our analysis reveals that a limited set of frequently used cryptocurrency addresses are responsible for creating currency trails, often from notorious cryptocurrency exchange platforms. We have further identified key entity types, including mixers, hacked victims, and suspicious wallet owners, which significantly contribute to trail creation. Moreover, we have observed that a small subset of currency trails lead to block height escalation, which may indicate more complex illicit activities. We have also developed a scoring system to quantify the susceptibility of each currency trail and provide a comprehensive classification that covers all trail types. Our research provides a foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of cryptocurrency-based blockchain security and trail analysis.

We have designed an novel coding scheme that utilizes reinforcement learning to deliver reliable quantum computations in the presence of quantum noise. This scheme involves using coding measurements in combination with channel reversal, allowing for the decoupling of error correction from computation. We successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this coding approach by accurately simulating its performance during both short-wave and long-wave noise exposure. Our code can be found on the CodeOcean platform for further exploration.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. A notable strategy, known as quantum leap metrology, involves using quantum correlations to achieve the most accurate measurements of a unknown variable by watching it change. This method has significant potential for applying energy-measuring tools, known as meters, to high-frequency processes. Here, we propose using a two-cavity system connected by an optical fiber to implement this strategy, and we outline the conditions and benefits of using this setup. This configuration allows us to use laser-based measurement tools known as interferometers, which can accurately measure changes in frequency, amplitude, and phase shifts. This research also identifies the conditions under which this setup can provide the most accurate measurements, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by accurately measuring key parameters of an optical fiber, including its length and the loss coefficient.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

Consider a positive integer n, whose digits of sigma(n) are denoted as s1, s2,...,sr, where r is the number of digits in sigma(n). We refer to the product of these digits as the general Smarandache's sigma multiplication of n, and it is denoted as S(n). This paper presents the concept of S(n) and explores its behavior through examples and tables, also addressing related recurrence and cyclic patterns.

The effectiveness of cloud-based applications is subject to fluctuating network conditions, which can pose a significant challenge to system scalability. To mitigate this obstacle, a comprehensive framework has been established to address and remedy the detrimental effects of network variability on system performance. This framework leverages a novel, multi-faceted approach that incorporates mathematical modeling and the development of energy-aware, self-adaptive applications. Furthermore, the practical viability of this framework is demonstrated through its integration with Hadoop, a widely adopted cloud computing platform. Experimental results show that network variability can impede system performance by at least 50%, while our proposed framework mitigates this decline, enabling scalable application execution even in the presence of significant network fluctuations.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where contextual information needs to be shared between decision makers and learners. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel approach that enables multiple agents to learn in a contextual linear bandit setting without sharing their individual context settings. This approach leverages the existing Linear Contextual Bandit algorithm and offers a regrettably suboptimal guarantee. Notably, this paper provides the first framework for addressing this challenge and its results are promising enough to warrant further research.

Over time, the trend of working from home has become increasingly common, also affecting software development projects. This study sets out to identify the influence of working from home on the success of Scrum projects using a multi-method approach, comprising both quantitative and qualitative data. The quantitative analysis of existing surveys revealed a significant correlation between working from home and the success of Scrum projects. Furthermore, in-depth interviews with software development teams confirmed that working from home can either positively or negatively impact the success of Scrum projects, depending on factors such as team dynamics and home environment. These findings have implications for project managers and organizations, and future research directions in this area are also outlined.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which introduces and analyzes a policy evaluation procedure related to ETE. We specifically explored and evaluated the performance of distributionally robust individualized treatment effects, which has been a widely researched topic in the recent past. Our work can be seen as building upon the foundation laid by Waggoner and Kallus (2020) and adapting the approach of Jiang et al. (2020) to create a practical solution for TRQ-learning via an efficient and trustworthy procedure. Our findings include the derivation of problem-specific bounds, validation of the effectiveness of the ROFTRQ procedure in a simulated environment, and a policy evaluation application using real-world data.

Our analysis manipulates the initial state of a similar system in a similar way, but with a twist that now affects the final state. We use a specific approach to examine how the elliptic flow coefficient is affected in a particular range of final states. The examination is performed using a set of collisions at a high energy, and the results are compared to a well-established theoretical model. We discovered that a particular feature of the final state can be linked to a specific feature of the initial state. This relationship holds true even when the influence of the collision process is factored in. We applied a similar approach to a different aspect of the final state, and found that its characteristics are influenced by an intricate interplay between two features of the initial state, and that this relationship is also affected by the collision process. This type of analysis provides valuable insights into the nature of a complex system in a state of high energy, and can be used to verify and refine a well-established theoretical model of this system.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a novel mathematical tool, derived from the Linear Canonical Transform. We then establish important properties and indeterminacy principles for the QLCT, extending the concepts of time and frequency analysis to the quaternion algebra. Specifically, we prove the QLCT preserves certain functions and is an isometry. Furthermore, we derive indeterminacy relations and a Heisenberg inequality for the QLCT, providing a deeper understanding of this transform and its relationship to traditional time and frequency analysis.

This work calculates the extreme sum rate benefits of optimal power control versus binary power control in an interference network with arbitrary power settings, and finds that this benefit is proportional to $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ as the number of users doubles. Additionally, we determine that the high-SNR extremal benefit of optimal power over binary power is precisely $\frac{K}{2}$, and this benefit increases to $\frac{2K\sqrt{K}-1}{2}$ as the number of users triples. Notably, we discover that the extremal benefit of optimal over binary power is not always maximized by the highest and lowest power settings - there are certain settings that provide a higher benefit, and these can be optimal in up to two-thirds of all interference networks. Furthermore, we find that the theta-function benefit is proportional to $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in all scenarios.

This study introduces an integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional particle methods can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing collision models often rely on integrating through the entire collision process at once, which can lead to unrealistic particle interactions. Our multiple-time-step integration method addresses these issues by allowing for simulation time steps that are longer than the collision time steps. This approach involves solving the flow simulation using large time steps and resolving particle collisions using smaller time steps. We leveraged this method to develop a particle-resolved simulation technique, which can accurately model a range of complex particle interactions, even in cases with large size ratios. This new method was tested against laboratory measurements and numerical models for two flow scenarios: the sedimentary layer formed by rolling grains and the turbulent sediment transport at a wall. Results show that our method can significantly reduce simulation time while maintaining high precision and is therefore an efficient approach for simulating particle flows.

This paper examines number theory by analyzing the factorization of a quadratic expression, specifically $a^2+ab+b^2$, and presents new proof for a conjecture related to whole number solutions of the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. We also explore related factorizations and examine whole number solutions for a similar equation with a base other than 7.

A key challenge in robotics is for lower body mechanisms to adapt to changing terrain dynamics.
As a solution, researchers are exploring robotics that incorporate flexible and dynamic interactions with their environment.
In this study, we focus on a single leg robotic system designed for horizontal surface exploration.
When the surface begins to yield under pressure, typically represented by an elliptical shape, the robot experiences a complex dynamic phenomenon.
To address this, we developed a mathematical model that takes into account both the robot's rigid structure and its hydraulic components.
The resulting simulation reveals how the monopod's movement can be optimized for maximum hopping distance.
Interestingly, our analysis shows that, despite being under significant dynamic stresses, the elliptical terrain can support an infinite number of harmonic vibrations.
Building on this finding, we developed an acoustic metamaterials-inspired approach to create a simplified terrain design capable of maximizing the robot's hopping range.
A corresponding simulation and experimental test bed validate the efficacy of this design.

In this paper, we revise a previous calculation of form factors for mesons using the $B\to \gamma$ decay amplitude. We specifically examine the processes $B\to (\pi,\rho)\gamma$ and $\eta\to \gamma\gamma$ to determine the form factors for the mesons $\pi$ and $\rho$, which are not directly observable in $\eta\to \gamma\gamma$ decay. Our analysis employs the light-cone distribution amplitude approach and perturbative QCD with the contour part being ignored. We calculate the amplitude for $B\to \gamma$ decay through the effective theory of heavy quarks and obtain the expression for the form factor. We then apply this to the $B\to (\pi,\rho)\gamma$ transition and find the form factor at the momentum transfer $q^2=0$. For the $\eta$ meson, we calculate the form factors for the decay $\eta\to \gamma\gamma$ by incorporating the contributions from quark annihilation and end-point region calculations. Our findings are in line with previous results for $\eta\to \gamma\gamma$ and $B\to \eta\gamma$.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a droplet charged by a nearby point source, our study sheds light on a previously unexamined scenario. We have a fan-like pattern observed when a droplet, suspended mid-way between two parallel electrodes, is close to an aerosolized charge source. By utilizing energy conservation and solving the Laplace equation, we numerically simulate and accurately replicate the experimental results. This includes the distinctive fan shape observed when the angle between the electrodes is 90 degrees. Furthermore, our analysis identifies two critical factors that influence this phenomenon: the EHD E-field and the gradient of the potential field. This study provides the foundation for further exploration of EHD-driven fluid dynamics within aerosolized environments.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all languages. Despite being ubiquitous, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to systematically present knowledge and effectively navigate complex networks. Despite their widespread use, there's a lack of research on efficient methods for computing and validating the efficacy of these frameworks, particularly in large-scale information networks. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a scoring system and set of algorithms for detecting and evaluating information hierarchies in networks, which we applied to a sample dataset and observed resulting hierarchies that were both coherent and easy to navigate.

In quantum annealing, a critical parameter is the annealing interval, denoted by $\epsilon$, as it significantly influences transition probability between ground and excited states. We have undertaken a detailed examination of this aspect in the context of an unbiased, unbiased-quenching variant of quantum annealing. Through both numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we have identified major dynamics associated with both quantum and quenching transitions. Our results indicate that in the quenching case, coherence is preserved as indicated by partial overlap between initial and final wavefunctions. In contrast, the ground state is fully recovered in the quantum case, albeit at a much slower pace. We have further derived the probability of remaining in the ground state in the quenching case, which exhibits an exponential decline with the number of qubits. Interestingly, this decline can be slowed down by increasing symmetry within the system. We have also observed an intriguing parallel between the probabilities of error in both quenching and quantum transitions, which demonstrates an exponential decrease with the square of the annealing interval.

Business processes are often modeled using techniques such as process mining and trace analysis, which rely on the use of transitions systems and alignments for comparing actual process behavior to expected patterns. The calculations involved can be computationally expensive, leading to difficulties in analyzing entire process runs. This paper explores the concept of analyzing partial process runs and presents efficient algorithms for calculating alignments using prefix and suffix comparisons of the runs, building on the foundation of existing work on infix alignments. The proposed methods can handle both deterministic and non-deterministic processes, as well as fair and unfair conformities, and offer significant improvements in accuracy over less sensitive alternatives. The techniques are demonstrated through application to real-world data sets, showing potential for broader integration into process mining tools.

Theories predicting d-wave superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelate typically rely on a single-band model containing d-orbitals, which doesn't account for p-orbitals present in the material. Using a two-band model including both p and d-orbitals, we show that strong correlations within the d-orbitals, mediated by strong Coulomb interactions and hybridization between the p and d-orbitals, are responsible for a phenomenon that increases the attractiveness of a site to an electron, counteracting its repulsion due to other electrons. This effect, called anti-screening, lengthens the time it takes for nickelate to lose superconductivity as more electrons are added. As a result, two-band model predictions for superconductivity are more accurate than those of a single-band model. We also find that the anti-screening effect could be relevant to other infinite-band materials near superconductivity.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By correcting existing errors and omissions in the literature, the paper demonstrates the following key conclusions for initial conditions with sufficiently low magnitudes: the solution's decay rate is determined by the collision operator's Landau operator and the dispersion associated with the projectable part of the linearized generator; the decay rate can be slowed by the influence of tangent frequencies within the Landau operator and the scattering operator's blending phase.

We use satellite data to study the relationship between wave slope and wind speed over the open ocean, investigating how this relationship changes in response to changing sea surface temperature. A statistical model is utilized to simulate the distribution of wave slopes under various wind conditions and temperatures. The results indicate that wave slopes exceed a certain threshold as wind speeds approach 18 m/s. Furthermore, the relationship between wave slopes and wind speeds is found to be more complex than previously suggested, with better fit to data when modeled as a cumulative distribution function rather than a linear function. Additionally, we found that increased sea surface temperature reduces the slope of waves at low to moderate wind speeds, and reduces the threshold at which waves start to slope excessively at higher wind speeds.

When designing a software system, altering its source code to facilitate parallel execution is a fundamental requirement. Nonetheless, this transformation alone is insufficient, as it's also necessary to recompile the software to optimize its performance in a parallel environment. This compilation process can be costly and inefficient when testing the software. Consequently, the paper presents an approach that utilizes Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to condense the software source code, thereby enabling parallel execution without the need for full recompilation. This approach is coupled with an SVD-based algorithm that facilitates efficient test case selection for the software. The proposed method is coupled with a case study that illustrates the efficacy of SVD in streamlining the test case choice algorithm. The results of the case study and subsequent evaluation indicate that the SVD-based algorithm is conducive to software development.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news on COVID-19, which is not only harmful but also hazardous. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of microblogging data has become a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce a sentiment analysis framework that enables the classification of Twitter data into positive, negative, and neutral categories. Furthermore, we present a contextualization approach for grading the sentiment of text on a scale from 0 to 5. This research is backed by an experimental study using a large coronavirus pandemic-related Twitter dataset, which includes around 10,000 text entries and their corresponding sentiment scores. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework, and it has the potential to contribute significantly to issues related to microblogging, sentiment analysis, and cross-domain learning.

Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. These models were particularly effective in understanding interlayer phase locking, critical current, and magnetic penetration depth. Nevertheless, the discovery of charge density waves in cuprates complicates the picture and necessitates a revised theoretical framework. In response, we have developed a broader tunneling model, incorporating charge density waves with a specific ratio of their spatial extent and interlayer separation. The revised model leads to the emergence of a longer interlayer length scale, distinct from both the Lawrence-Doniach and intra/interlayer lengths, which is in line with recent observations. Consequently, a longer interlayer critical current, reduced interlayer coupling, and a specific relationship between the critical current and the Lawrence-Doniach length scale are predicted. These predictions provide a foundation for a thorough examination of charge density waves in cuprates through transport and interlayer studies.

The adiabatic index of matter determines how the volume of matter changes in response to temperature changes, influencing the stability of neutron stars. The index's behavior varies based on the density of matter, especially in its core, where dense matter with strange quarks may exist within neutron stars. In this study, we examine the sonic point, located where the speed of sound equals the rotational frequency of a rotating neutron star, particularly in its dense core. The speed of sound in dense matter with strange quarks and adiabatic indices greater than 2 is not significantly impacted by the presence of strange quark condensates, as other effects may influence it more. However, when the index is close to 2, the speed of sound can be larger than the speed of light, as predicted by general relativity, and may be impacted by the strange quark condensates' effects on the index itself.

The anti-Tai mapping concept was initially introduced in relation to ordered trees with distinct node labels arranged in ascending order. This study expands the idea to its application in disordered labeled trees. By reviewing existing theories and identifying relevant patterns, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the anti-Tai mapping framework across various domains, including recursive structures, context-free grammars, and monoids. Furthermore, this study introduces novel acceptance conditions for disordered trees based on the anti-Tai mapping principle and correlates these conditions with Chomsky hierarchies, specifically recognizing the class of context-sensitive languages and expanding the scope of recursively generated language families.

We investigate what happens to a coherent state as its Gaussian Wigner function transforms both in phase space and in the number state representation. Our analysis utilizes an extended phase-space transformation that includes a linear shift. Our calculations yield a rotated coherent state, obtainable by adjusting a complex transformation matrix associated with the original coherent state. Our study demonstrates that both the number-average and the variance of the number operator remain constant under this transformation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the case of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, this transformation represents a rotation in phase space, whereas in the case of a Kerr oscillator, additional compression and displacement effects arise, influencing the average number of photons and the variance of the photon number.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems. It is triggered by the interaction of different rotation speeds in the horizontal plane and is further exacerbated by the presence of a non-zero shear component in the vertical direction. Previous studies on VSI have been based on ideal gas assumptions, but since dust plays a significant role in the physical properties of these systems, it's essential to analyze its effect on VSI. We examined the stability of protoplanetary disk systems by taking into account the behavioral changes of dust as it travels from the inner regions towards the outer regions. Our analysis revealed that dust undergoes a phase change from large particles in the inner regions to smaller grains in the outer regions, a process influenced by the temperature and location within the alpha disk. The impact of dust evolution on VSI was then analyzed through a one-dimensional disk model, showing that as dust grain sizes decrease, the sound speed also decreases, eventually reaching a point where it becomes small enough to support VSI in the outer regions of the disk. This decrease in sound speed is attributed to the changing electrical conductivity and magnetic Prandtl number as grain sizes decrease, which in turn affects the angular momentum transport mechanism. The results of our analysis suggest that VSI can occur in the outer regions of a disk due to the behavioral changes of dust over time.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant, without the need for compactness or other additional assumptions. We demonstrate that bounded harmonic functions are constant, and this conclusion has significant implications for the study of a related equation. The results presented in this work build upon earlier findings by Hamilton, Li, and Ni, and the approach involves a combination of analysis and geometric reasoning.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even with a relatively small amount of compromised training data, hidden functionalities could be incorporated into a neural network, particularly in situations where the network is trained from a vast amount of diverse data. In fact, it has been observed that such techniques could be employed even when the backdoor is isolated from primary network functions. Interestingly, hidden functionalities could also be incorporated more easily into certain neural network architecture such as attention based networks and multi-layer networks, than others. Furthermore, it has been found that these techniques could be applied across a wide range of applications such as sound, text, and image classification. In conclusion, incorporating hidden functionalities into a neural network through compromised training data poses a significant threat to machine learning systems.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses potential distortions in Gaia-like spacecraft data, caused by large-scale distortions in space-time. Researchers examine the impact of an unknown post-Newtonian constant on parallax measurements, which could be significant, with errors as large as 0.5 microarcseconds. Therefore, tightly constrained post-Newtonian parameters are essential for fully utilizing the precision of future global astronomical catalogs.

We have developed an efficient approach for significantly reducing the complexity of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems using their recent recent observations. The method leverages time-series data and algorithms to identify a lower-dimensional structure within the system, then rapidly generates a highly simplified model that accurately captures the system's behavior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to two complex systems: a model for lung expansion and a vascular network. In the lungs model, we successfully reduce the dimensionality by 99% while maintaining precise predictions; in the vascular network, we achieve a 5-fold reduction in dimensions. Furthermore, we provide an open-source software framework that can handle systems with both observed and unobserved components.

In model systems with high-frequency modulation, solitons are normally destroyed due to phase and amplitude locking. Notably, Bose-Einstein condensates subjected to high-frequency periodic forces exhibit an exceptional phenomenon, where unstable waves can be stabilized if our method of applied field is abrupt rather than smooth. This leads to the creation of solitary waves that can increase in power as the intensity of the periodic force is elevated, a phenomenon that these waves exhibit and that cannot be seen in conventional methods. This implies that these waves can select up energy from the model system, making them self-sustaining. This feature is displayed through BEC models and theory, and it also appears in other systems that can be modeled with a complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. This phenomenon is shown to result from a subtle interaction between frequency locking and release in the amplitude and phase of an unstable wave, and it can be used to create stable, self-sustaining waves in model systems that normally cannot support solitons.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies have been conducted on this issue, they have not yet been extensively researched. Our work Concentration Inequality for Adaptive Attacks (CIAA) is the first to deeply explore this problem and provides solutions for it. Specifically, we propose an enhanced protocol called SIMC 2.0 that significantly improves the previous SIMC protocol in several areas. Firstly, SIMC 2.0 can handle a wider range of noise concentration inequalities than SIMC. Secondly, it reduces the amount of communication between the client and server by half. Thirdly, it provides more accurate error bounds for a longer period of time. Moreover, we show that SIMC 2.0 is more efficient than previous protocols like HSIMC and TFDI in terms of communication cost. Moreover, CIAA and SIMC 2.0 can be applied to a broader class of forward-compatibility attacks, and the former is related to a statistical theory problem.

Our research includes a large-scale HI intensity mapping experiment using the FAST radio telescope, which allows us to discover an extended, thin HI cloud and a HI tail in the M101 galaxy group. These findings were derived from 343 frequency bands, each with a width of 40.4 kHz, and total integration times of 2.56 and 5.12 hours for the 34 and 19 frequency bands respectively. Our data have a resolution of 327.4 MHz in frequency and 408.000 km/s in velocity, as well as a resolution of 324.5716 km/s in velocity and 3.82 arcmin in width. From our data, we detected an HI signal at a significance level of more than 3.5 sigma, with a total mass of approximately 7.10 10^8 M. Our analysis includes a spatial width of about 11.5 kpc and a peak systemic velocity of about 655.2 km/s. Additionally, we observed an HI cloud with a total mass of about 1.59 10^9 M, located about 76.7 kpc from its main HI component and separated from it by about 43.1 kpc in velocity. Our results also show an HI tail with a total mass of about 1.59 10^9 M, extending about 76.7 kpc from its main HI component and separated from it by about 656.1 kpc in space

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing vast knowledge typically leads to noise and ambiguity issues. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven approach to enrich the answer candidate generation process. Initially, we perform a coarse-grained search for answers based on the question's semantics, narrowing down the knowledge to a limited set of relevant concepts. Subsequently, we conduct a more meticulous analysis to generate new answer candidates, drawing from these concepts and a broader knowledge base. We integrate this approach into a unified framework for commonsense question answering, achieving notable improvements over baseline methods and establishing new state-of-the-art performance on CommonsenseQA and Commonsense Reasoning.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength emission than their neutral counterparts, existing spectral models are predominantly based on the properties of neutral molecules. As a result, there are significant knowledge gaps in the spectra of oxygen-containing molecular cions. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the spectra of these molecular cations, with a particular focus on the electron excitation spectra and the emission spectra after non-radioactive decay. Specifically, we have undertaken an in-depth investigation of six oxygen-containing molecular cations, specifically CO+, CO2+, CS+, CS2+, OCS+ and CS2+ with variations in isoelectronic systems, to establish a more robust understanding of their emission spectra and how they relate to the spectra of neutral molecules and common astronomical ions.

We present a novel algorithm for determining whether a given integer combination of unity squares (a "sum of squares") can be expressed as a sum of integers, a phenomenon known as "positive semi-definiteness". This algorithm also identifies the minimum integer values needed in such a representation. Additionally, we extend this capability to "sums of norms", a type of integer combination of higher-dimensional regular polygons with prime edge lengths. Sertöz and Brightwater previously developed an iterative method for analyzing "sums of squares". In contrast, our new approach introduces a novel algorithmic method for "positive semi-definite analysis of squares and norms" in global fields, including the fields of rational numbers, Gaussian rationals, and finite fields.

Recent developments in photonic technology offer innovative solutions to accurately measure molecular line spectra, which are crucial in astronomical research. This work presents a novel photonic device, capable of perfectly mimicking the principles of 1D spectrometers using a parallel array of waveguides. We demonstrate that this device can accurately calculate complex line profiles and efficiently process large amounts of data. Furthermore, we propose an easy-to-fabricate design based on a simple attenuation model, which can also minimize optical nonlinearities. These features make this device an ideal testbed for developing new, high-performance astrophotonic systems that integrate light sources and targets for spectral analysis.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

The classic Itô-Wentzell formula serves as a significant expansion of Itô's formula, enabling its application to functions that are not differentiable. We have obtained a generalized version of this formula, adapted to functionals with bumps in their derivatives, which can be seen as a further development of the Yang-Zhou free flow Itô-Wentzell formula. Moreover, we have established that the solution to which it applies can be represented in an explicit and integrable manner. Additionally, we have derived a generalized version of the Itô-Wentzell formula for paths with p-variation less than one-half, for which we have also established the integrability of the derivative.

In a context where data privacy restrictions limit access to sensitive information, an alternative approach to training models involves leveraging samples from a larger, unlabelled pool of data points. This paper presents a novel, random walk method for federated learning that takes advantage of unlabelled data and reduces communication between nodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy in a setting inspired by the Labeled Large-Sample Learning problem. We also showcase the practical applicability of our method by using the San Francisco Bay Area as a case study and comparing its performance to baseline methods. This involves compiling a dataset from Homestead VA mapping platform and openly available information about places. We assess the performance of this method in a setting inspired by the Labeled Large-Sample Learning problem and a simulation of a FL setting.

Three-dimensional deep water wave turbulence is examined in this study for its energy density distribution. Previous experiments and computations by Zakharov, Bieliakov and Kolmogorov all indicated that energy follows a specific scaling, but only remained accurate for a limited range of frequencies. Our current research utilizes large-scale numerical models to reevaluate frequency spectra and reveals that the scaling holds true across a wider range of frequencies than previously recorded. A notable increase in energy accumulation at very low frequencies was also observed and could be linked to the inherent bias in traditional methods of data analysis.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the criminal justice system.  The research focuses on offenders sentenced to probation rather than incarceration and finds that mental health treatment reduces the risk of rearrest by 17% within a three-year time frame and 24% within six years.  This reduction in recidivism risk is seen across various mental health conditions, with the greatest benefits observed for individuals with substance abuse disorders, anxiety/depressive disorders, and attention deficit and hyperactivity disorders.  Notably, offenders who completed treatment had a lower risk of rearrest compared to those who did not, with risk decreasing by as much as 23% within three years.  These findings offer empirical support for mandated mental health treatment as part of community supervision and suggest it may be more effective when required by the court rather than offered voluntarily.

A burgeoning area in medical image analysis, semi-supervised learning uses a limited set of labeled images in conjunction with a vast amount of unlabeled data to improve model performance and accuracy. To overcome existing challenges, we propose an unconventional approach to regularization, one that involves modeling real-world images as a combination of distinct components, including background noise and visually meaningful objects. This regularization technique is based on the principle of using a realistic object mask to weight the model's prediction, effectively eliminating unnecessary transformations and ensuring that predictions conform to the original image characteristics. We further develop a novel, unbiased sampling method to securely utilize unlabeled images, thus preventing potential model biases. By integrating these techniques, we demonstrate significant improvements in modeling real-world images and variety. Notably, our method surpasses leading approaches in the domain, achieving remarkable accuracy on benchmark datasets.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade of the LHC's detector system. As part of this upgrade, the Level 1 Jet Calorimeter Trigger (JETT) system will utilize new hardware based on an ATCA and Ultrascale+ FPGAs design, in order to enhance its speed and accuracy. The new board, designed by an international collaboration of researchers, will employ four high-speed processors and a calorimeter data concentrator to improve the system's performance and efficiency. This paper will provide an in-depth overview of the new board's design, its expected benefits, and the reasoning behind its design. Furthermore, it will outline the ongoing development process and the remaining challenges to be addressed before the upgrade is complete.

Our project involves creating a groundbreaking new technology that transforms the traditional static avatars used in virtual environments into dynamic, realistic representations of human beings, complete with articulated skeletons and detailed facial expressions generated through a generative adversarial network. Building upon cutting-edge AI developments, we aim to further advance this field by integrating our technology into popular online platforms, enabling seamless and immersive virtual interactions between users. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of our research and presents a novel solution for producing high-quality, articulated avatar images through a combined effort of generative adversarial networks and neural 3D rendering tools.

Paradoxically, complex quantum systems with high dimensions of freedom require more precise knowledge of individual particle movements. In this case, we applied graph neural networks to an exactly integrable one-dimensional model of freely moving atoms, and found that their reliance on particle interactions for prediction errors significantly highlights the inherent chaos of the system when internal correlations are lacking. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the simplicity of this system allows for a deeper understanding of how chaos is influenced by both these internal correlations and the random movement of the atoms.

Consider a situation with unknown probability distribution P mixing known distributions Q(y|θ) parameterized by θ, where a single observation Y is used to estimate the average of the mixing probabilities or distribution parameters. The objective is to maximize the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of a function of P, specifically expectations of functionals of P or its parameters, which is referred to as generalized maximum likelihood estimation (GMLE). A notable application arises in sampling, where we aim to estimate the expected payoff of a random mixture of unknown probability distribution. By leveraging the R\'enyi divergence, we derive a variational lower bound that facilitates the computation of GMLEs, making it a viable solution for complex problems. Theoretical guarantees are established for convergent iterations and the accuracy of the proposed method, and it is shown that it is comparable to the standard maximum likelihood estimation method under certain conditions. The method is then illustrated through an analysis of a sampling scenario, as well as simulations and real-world experiments using neural network-based generative models.

Knowledge tracing has emerged as a significant application at the intersection of online learning analysis and artificial intelligence, which we refer to as the IQ graph. This graph represents the relationships between learning platforms, data, and models. In this paper, we introduce pyKT, an open-source Python library designed to guide researchers through the evaluation of knowledge tracing models, especially those utilizing neural networks and machine learning. Additionally, pyKT provides an accessible platform for researchers to easily experiment with their own methods within this context.

Given a polynomial mapping $f$ from an open set in $\mathbb{C}^n$ to $\mathbb{C}^m$, we demonstrate that the range of the associated invariant differential operator $E$ is the entire space of holomorphic functions, provided that $f$ does not map any non-empty open subset of $\mathbb{C}^n$ onto a compact variety. This result has notable implications for several questions in the study of several complex variables and complex analysis.

In this extended abstract, we present Alethe, a cutting-edge, versatile DPLL(T) solver developed with the aim of providing a common framework that encompasses a broad spectrum of SMT solvers. Alethe's core consists of a modular design, comprising multiple theories that can be seamlessly integrated. Its solver core, based on DPLL(T), can efficiently resolve problems by leveraging the individual theories. Furthermore, Alethe's design includes an innovative strategy to handle conflicts and extensions, enabling it to work optimally with its component theories. We demonstrate Alethe's effectiveness through a set of challenging benchmarks, showcasing its superior performance. Additionally, we present Alethe's source code and executable version for further exploration and customization.

As the number of devices contributing to federated learning grows, synchronizing updates becomes less efficient. A common remedy involves using a central aggregator to coordinate, yet this can lead to suboptimal performance by restricting gradient updates. We explore an alternative approach, experimenting with unrestricted gradients in a context where devices update asynchronously and aggregate locally. Our results show that this method yields faster convergence and more accurate outcomes, especially when the number of participating devices is large. We also introduce a novel, self-adaptive technique for setting learning rates and validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, essentially mapping one language's speech-to-text task to another. This approach has shown success with the use of multilingual models, particularly in low-resource scenario situations. We explored this concept using a German dataset, initially developing a German ASR system from scratch, which struggled due to limited data availability. We managed to improve this base system through the application of transfer learning, first by fine-tuning a pre-trained German model and subsequently a German model that supported additional languages. We also examined the possibility of using German text-to-text translation for cross-lingual ASR, initially achieving poorer results but eventually achieving a significant drop in word error rate.

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Players, has been created by extracting a vast range of information from the Twitch gaming platform. This dataset encompasses 1,441 users with 12 million interactions over a 12-month period and is characterized by shifting community structures and user engagement patterns. Experimental comparisons using multiple node embedding methods confirm that Twitch Players offers a rigorous framework for evaluating the effectiveness of novel node embedding algorithms, capable of withstanding adjustments to hyperparameters.

Our study proposes that a previously observed resonance, $f_X(1500)$, might actually be a higher spin state of the $\rho^0$ resonance at $1450$, and we perform a comprehensive analysis of $B\to \pi(K)KK$ decays to test this hypothesis. We derive tight constraints on the product of the $\rho^0(1450)$ decay width and branching ratio to the $KK$ channel, which could be as low as $2.3\times 10^{-5}$ GeV, and we estimate that with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ of $B$-barrel data, the LHCb detector can detect a $\rho^0(1450)$ signal with $5$ $\sigma$ confidence at a mass point of $1499.7$ MeV. If this signal is observed, we can also determine the $\rho^0(1450)$ spin, and we show that with $20$ ab$^{-1}$ of $B$-barrel data, the spin can be distinguished with $1.5\sigma$ confidence. If the $\rho^0(1450)$ is indeed a high spin state, and considering the $J^P=4^-$ assignment, we find that the $f_X(1500)$ detection could be confirmed with $6.2\sigma$ confidence.

Recent cosmological and particle physics standards suggest a dark matter component made up of 1-30 solar mass black holes. We explored the possibility of an additional, "dark" dimension in a scenario where these heavy black holes, capable of interacting with our own dimension only through gravitation, exist. We determined that the existence of such a extra dimension is consistent with the constraints imposed by the Swampland program. Furthermore, we found that a dark dimension of this nature can explain the observed lack of binary black hole mergers in our own dimension, and that it has a minor impact on the large-scale structure of the universe. Additionally, we found that a dark dimension does not conflict with the gravitational wave observations from a single event, such as a compact object merger involving a primordial black hole of mass $379_{-26}^{+43}$ solar masses.

A key issue in Series Elastic Actuators (SEAs) is accurate force control. To tackle this challenge, a novel force estimation technique is introduced, based on a approach that utilizes the elastic module's measurement and the actuator's measurement to calculate the transmission force. The transmission force is the force transmitted by the actuator's motor to its link. A comparison of the proposed method, referred to as the transmission force observer, is made with the established approach of using the elastic module's measurement alone. The results of the comparison, involving the manipulation of the actuator's friction and the introduction of a force disturbance, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method. The latter's superiority is attributed to its ability to accurately estimate the transmission force even in the presence of varying actuator friction.

A distinct feature of living rafts, comprising cells that are linked and attached at specific points, is the appearance of clear gaps when they are viewed under a microscope. These gaps can provide crucial information about the composition of cell junctions and adhesion networks, and their size can be quantitatively measured in various systems using advanced image analysis techniques. In this study, we examine in detail the size distribution of gaps within colonies of E. coli by controlling key factors including cell density, age, and the presence of nutrients. Our analysis reveals a significant gap size difference of up to ten-fold, and we propose that this variation could significantly impact the colony's ability to withstand external forces. To better understand the interplay between cell adhesion and mechanical stress, we develop and validate a mathematical model that accurately predicts observed gap size distributions in our experiments and in previously published photographs.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are present at multiple possible symmetry-breaking directions corresponding to different phases of the theory. Our study employs an extensive Monte Carlo simulation to investigate the phase diagram and Higgs phases of this complex system. Our results first identify the critical temperatures for both the deconfinement and Higgs transition temperatures. We've found that at the origin of the phase diagram, the Higgs phase is confined to a narrow angle that increases with Nc. This confinement is caused by the interaction between the scalar fields and the fundamental gauge fields. Additionally, our results indicate that for certain angles within the Higgs phase region, the scalar fields may undergo a symmetry-restoring transition through a mean-field-like behavior, characterized by the formation of distinct condensates that break the SU(Nc) symmetry.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges in training a marine robot to follow instructions. We've discovered that using a Gaussian Process regression model and aQP solver in a TD framework is highly effective, and this effectiveness is further enhanced by incorporating a sparse approximation technique. Our model's sparse implementation not only significantly reduces memory requirements but also accelerates its training process. We've conducted a comprehensive set of experiments to validate our method and a key finding from these experiments is the striking contrast between the model's performance and its simplicity. Our approach has achieved very promising results and we believe our work will be a valuable reference for researchers exploring TD learning in more complex and diverse settings.

This paper introduces a novel class of arranging networks with limited depth. Unlike traditional neural network architectures where arrangement axes are implicitly assumed to be linear, our model allows for non-linear data projection. We present a specific implementation utilizing constant-depth ReLU units, demonstrating that this arrangement model is comparable to a stacked linear network. Furthermore, we show that the constant-depth arranging network achieves comparable performance to its deep linear counterpart, while also being computationally efficient and easily optimized for small data sets.

We investigate a relativistic star with anisotropic matter, assuming that
the pressure gradient affects the motion of matter.  By employing a linear
approach, we derive an exact solution for the metric within the framework of
General Relativity.  Our solution is valid for both non-rotating and rotating
stars.  For the purpose of verification, we compare our results with those
obtained using the relaxation method in Numerical Relativity.  Specifically,
we examine the behavior of both anisotropic and isotropic stars, including
those with high densities.  Our findings are in alignment with the expectations
of the series expansion method and reveal minimal discrepancies when comparing
results from both approaches for energy densities up to $\rho \approx 8.5\rho_c$.

The observed spiral structure in a galaxy resembles a grand design spiral pattern, yet for a long time, researchers have struggled to model its behavior due to the absence of a fundamental law governing the formation of spiral patterns. This phenomenon was recently explained by a group of scientists who discovered that a two-dimensional, collisionless N-body model could be used to map the spiral pattern of a galaxy by identifying periodic orbits and tracking the motion of particles within it. In this paper, a more comprehensive approach is presented, based on a model that includes a bulge, a dark matter halo, and multiple components, similar to those found in the Milky Way. Rather than relying on a simple particle dynamics simulation, a numerical technique was employed to solve a system of ordinary differential equations, derived from the assumptions of a collisionless N-body universe, and resulting in a set of Fokker-Planck-Boltzmann equations. By using this method, a high-resolution map of the galaxy was created, and the existence of a closed curve, representing a stable periodic orbit, was confirmed through an analytical approach, and also by numerical and experimental means. This provides a foundation for more complex spiral structure modeling, and may contribute to a better understanding of the formation and behavior of galaxies in the universe.

In the current cosmic framework, galaxy mergers are guided by gravity alone. However, magnetic fields potentially play a significant role in shaping galaxy mergers, especially during major collisions. This study utilizes high-resolution SPH simulations to examine how magnetic fields affect the interaction between two identical galaxies colliding at various relative velocities, ranging from slow to highly energetic impacts. Our analysis reveals substantial influences of magnetic fields on the structure and movement of gas and stellar discs throughout the merger process. For high-velocity mergers, magnetic fields hinder the formation of massive, centrally-located star-forming regions by suppressing gas compression and forcing it instead to collapse at greater radii, resulting in the creation of ring-like features composed of both gas and stars. Furthermore, our findings indicate that magnetic fields cause warps in the discs of both galaxies, and this effect is more pronounced in lower-velocity mergers. This phenomenon is attributed to an increased dynamical influence on the inner regions during slower mergers, and it is expected that such magnetic field-driven feature patterns could be observed in remote galaxy mergers.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network (CMC). This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to accurately identify lung tissue and encodings within the CT images. These interpretations were then used to extract infection-aware 3D feature maps from pre-trained networks. To further enhance performance, we developed a Contrastive Mixup Classification framework that leverages these maps to capture COVID-19 characteristics and output the correct grade. Notably, our team ranked 1st in the COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition with a score of 0.7946, out of 1.0.

Many languages possess complex grammatical systems which can make native speaker-powered correction challenging and costly to implement. Native speaker models can be trained to correct specific languages, but their ability to correct other languages with similar grammatical structures is unexplored. We investigated if the similarities within language families can facilitate the transfer of correction skills. The results indicated that models can easily learn to correct languages with similar grammatical foundations, but difficult for them to learn to correct languages with distinct foundations. We discovered that models can efficiently learn to correct multiple languages within the same family with fewer data and training compared to models trained for a single language. Furthermore, ensembles of these highly-tuned models also demonstrated the ability to correct new languages from the same family with just a small amount of new data, a capability that was not observable with models trained on multiple languages simultaneously.

The practice of rounding numbers to the nearest integer is a widespread phenomenon, affecting survey respondents, self-reported data, and categorical measurements. This paper examines how this behavior affects the estimation of population counts using rounded averages, specifically when those estimates are based on a sample of ambiguous values. Our analysis shows that standard methods of inference can significantly overestimate confidence intervals due to the inherent ambiguity, leading to an unwanted increase in type I errors. We present a novel approach using an empirical Bayesian technique that accommodates this ambiguity and can reduce type I errors by as much as 36%. This new method is compared to existing strategies in a simulation study and is shown to be particularly beneficial in scenarios where ambiguity is more pronounced. The empirical implications of this research are relevant to any field involving self-reported data or categorical measurements, and we provide a case study using data from a prominent election survey.

We investigated the magnetic characteristics of the one-dimensional and two-dimensional centered honeycomb structures in GdInO3 using inelastic neutron scattering and specific heat measurements. By analyzing these properties, we found that GdInO3 exhibits long-range antiferromagnetic order below its Néel temperature T_N = 2.8 K, and we investigated the local and average magnetic arrangements within this ordered state. Additionally, we compared these arrangements to those predicted by a spin Hamiltonian model, and we identified a very small Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction energy in GdInO3. Moreover, we observed that the heat capacity is dominated by the Schottky anomaly from the low-lying Gd3+ levels and that it follows a damped sinusoidal pattern as it transitions from the antiferromagnetic to the paramagnetic state.

The proposed mechanism, known as the Indivisible Good Mechanism (IGM), allocates critical items to self-interested agents, where the mechanism's equilibria and fairness properties are to be examined. Specifically, the IGM targets items that cannot be divided, and agents rank the items based on their personal preferences. The mechanism's purity guarantees that no agent can benefit from a deviation, and this property is referred to as a pure Nash equilibrium. The distribution resulting from the IGM is considered fair if it is close to the most preferred equilibrium outcome achievable by the agents. The study's key contributions are as follows: (1) The existence of pure Nash equilibria is proven for the IGM in environments where agents' preferences are expressed through subadditive functions, and (2) The fairness of the IGM is ensured when the agents' preferences are orthogonally decomposed into additive components, and an approximation bound is derived for subadditive functions. The findings are illustrated through a series of fair-inference experiments on a variety of preference domains. The proposed mechanism is efficient, with an equilibrium time of O(n^2.5), and the IGM's fairness guarantees are shown to be men-by-approaching optimal for a broad category of subadditive functions.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct, one-to-one mapping between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic transformations to bridge the domains. This approach allows us to draw upon a vast array of transformation techniques available, going beyond the limitations of explicit domain coupling methods. We evaluate our strategy using both low-level data augmentation and learning-based transformations in the context of semantic segmentation, achieving superior results compared to the state-of-the-art approaches using both methods.

A massive, rotating disk in UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy with minimal bright central core, presents an intriguing spiral arm pattern. Despite initial assessments as a double galaxy, UGC 8839 remains a singular object with no discernible companion. Hubble Space Telescope observations reveal a disk exceptional for its low central brightness and stability across multiple wavelength ranges. Additionally, a lack of central massive black hole candidate and high stellar disk-to-bulge mass ratio contribute to its unique characteristics. UGC 8839 presents a rare opportunity to study a spiral galaxy's disk shaped by gravitational forces, as its bulge is remarkably low in mass.

Researchers are exploring a novel detection technique called "paleo-detectors" to identify dark matter, which involves studying the damage caused by dark matter particles in olivine crystals within ancient rocks, specifically from the Paleozoic era. These detectors have a distinct capability to detect the low-energy events induced by the scattering of dark matter particles with nucleons, a process called "solar dark matter." Furthermore, paleo-detectors can simultaneously investigate two important problems in geophysics, such as understanding the unexpected heat death of the solar system's innermost planets during the Goldilocks era and the sudden slowdown of these planets's rotation rates in the Mesozoic era. If successful, this technique could provide the first direct evidence for the existence of dark matter.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through the 'DP-schedule' approach. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, incorporates differential privacy into the 'update pattern leakage' of encrypted databases, ensuring the security of various types of databases, including graph, tree, and multi-tree databases. Additionally, DP-Sync provides query execution efficiency comparable to unsecured databases, with minor overhead due to the application of differential privacy.

The evaluation of feature importance in a machine learning model, particularly for the Random Forest algorithm, is a topic of ongoing research. This study introduces an innovative approach to assess feature significance based on feature contribution to the model's uncertainty calculation, specifically using the Mean Squared Error of the confidence scores. The proposed method is experimentally verified on various datasets and compared to the existing feature importance metrics of Random Forest, revealing that the approaches have distinct patterns and can provide valuable insights into model behavior and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial data.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning methods to automatically identify surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our approach showed that a combination of U-Net and RNN improved instrument detection accuracy, outperforming other deep learning networks. Our study aims to provide a foundation for the development of a fully automated system for monitoring surgical instruments and other abdominal organs during laparoscopic surgery.

The task of re-identifying individuals across different video cameras from the same event, based on extracted feature vectors, has not been effectively solved despite its crucial applications in crime investigation and security monitoring. This re-id challenge is exacerbated by the large number of potentially identifiable individuals involved. In an effort to address this issue, a new approach to data augmentation was developed, centered on a contrastive learning framework, which successfully scaled up the re-id process for large numbers of individuals. Furthermore, our proposed method was evaluated on a newly created, large-scale, unsupervised re-id dataset, and the results showed significant improvements over existing techniques.

This paper introduces an original model that uses a unique threshold assessment framework to analyze high-frequency financial data, incorporating a complex system for predicting tail risks. This new model, called BRTH-GARCH, delves into the unknown parameters of the model using a method called the Monte Carlo Markov Chain. Our study shows that the BRTH-GARCH model is exceptionally effective at forecasting tail risks, surpassing established competing models including the Financial Network GARCH and LEVY-GARCH models.
